docstring:
The fourth quarter is the one quarter no filing reports directly.

A company files three 10-Qs and then a 10-K. The 10-K covers the year, so the
fourth quarter has no filing of its own and an analyst who wants it has to take
the year less the nine months already reported. The tagged data says the same
thing: of the 5,524 annual filings in this window, 5,170 carry a year-to-date
net income and only 268 carry a quarterly one.

That the derivation is the right one is checkable rather than assumed. On the
256 filings that do carry both, the year less the paired nine months reproduces
the disclosed quarterly figure to the dollar 214 times, including at scale:
Accenture's 7,264,787,000 less 5,580,486,000 is the 1,684,301,000 it tags, and
AbbVie's -22,000,000 comes out of 4,278,000,000 less 4,300,000,000. No match is
degenerate; not one of the 214 has a nine-month figure of zero.

The remaining 42 are the point of the case. The derivation inherits every
restatement, reclassification and discontinued operation booked between the
third-quarter filing and the 10-K, and the two figures then disagree with no
way to say from these fields alone which one an analyst should carry. Five of
the 42 are a tagging fault visible without judgement, the annual figure sitting
in the quarterly slot: North Haven Private Income Fund tags 259,971,000 as its
quarter, which is exactly its year. The other 37 differ for reasons the fields
do not record, Ally Financial by 248,000,000 the widest among them.

Four conventions, each of which moves a reported number:

1. Fiscal years are selected by period end falling in calendar 2024, not by the
   ``fiscal_year`` label. The label puts two different fiscal years under 2024
   for the 52/53-week filers, so Children's Place appears under it for both the
   year ended 2024-02-03 and the year ended 2025-02-01. Selecting on the label
   gives 5,504 filers against 5,524. Seven filers still close twice inside
   calendar 2024 and the later period end is the fiscal 2024 one, while two
   more file the same period end twice; retaining the earlier row instead of
   the later gives 488.831902 rather than 488.833662 USD billions.
2. The paired nine-month filing is the Q3 10-Q whose period end is nearest
   before the annual period end and no more than 120 days before it. Without
   the cap a filer that skipped its third-quarter filing pairs against a much
   older one, which raises the derived total to 491.108491.
3. Amendments are outside the population on both sides. Admitting 10-K/A gives
   490.578436 and admitting 10-Q/A gives 488.946485.
4. Agreement is an absolute difference below one dollar. This one changes
   nothing measured here, the 42 disagreements being the same set under exact
   inequality; it is stated so the comparison survives float arithmetic rather
   than to admit a second reading.

Two selections the query leaves open because the data closes them. One paired
filer files its third-quarter period end twice and both rows carry the same
nine-month figure, so which row is taken does not reach a reported number. And
no filer has two third-quarter period ends inside the 120-day window, so the
nearest-filing rule never has to choose. The query still states the rule, since
a solver cannot know either of these before computing. The two tie-breaks that
do not fire are stated for the same reason and asserted not to fire in the
case-local test: no filer needs an accession to separate its annual rows, and
the widest disagreement leads the second by 27,000,000.

What the derivation rests on is dated and revisable. The submission index
matches 5,522 of these filings on filer and accession together, 85 of the
accessions being filed jointly by several filers so that the accession alone
duplicates rows. 574 of the filings are later superseded by an amendment for
the same period end, and the median gap from period end to public acceptance
is 65 days. Two filings the statements extract labels 10-K the index labels
10-K/A, neither field being checked against the other.

Revenue is not used. Only 1,945 of the annual filings tag a year-to-date
revenue and 91 a quarterly one, too thin a validation set to carry the same
argument.

The annual population is read from the financial statements, which the query
names, because the filing index lists filings that carry no statement row: its
unamended 10-Ks with a 2024 period end come from 5,711 filers against the 5,524
here, and turn five's form comparison only means something when the statements
are the side being checked.

Reconcile Apple's disclosed commitment ladders and run a curve sensitivity.

This is a hard baseline with explicit fact-grain audit outputs.  The measured alternatives retain both a physical-row sum and a distinct-value sum as measured wrong
paths, plus the dimensioned-component sum as a documented numerical equivalent.
Those alternatives test the XBRL surface without misclassifying a prompt that
asks the analyst to interpret its row-grain evidence as a diagnostic trap.

Gross debt is the face amount, which the query defines, not the net carrying
amount. The filing reports both: the face amount on four rows, two of them
undimensioned and both 91.281 billion, and the net carrying amount on a single
undimensioned row of 90.678 billion. The 0.603 billion between them is the
unamortized discount and issuance costs (0.309) and the hedge-accounting
adjustments. Reading the net figure reports counts of 1, 1 and 1, a gross of
90.678 and a difference of 603.0 million where the face amount reconciles to 0.0.

docstring:
Compare April MIDAS odd-lot scale with FINRA short-volume share.

Across 6,516 tickers present on every one of the 21 common April 2025 trading
dates, the top five by aggregate MIDAS odd-lot volume are NVDA, TSLA, SPY, PLTR
and AAPL.  NVDA leads absolute odd-lot volume at 0.466144230 billion shares, but
PLTR ranks fourth on that measure and has the cohort's highest FINRA short-volume
share at 59.6526%.  Ranking by MIDAS trade volume or equal-weighted row ratios,
using raw ticker-string equality instead of the pinned dot-to-slash share-class
bridge, or adding short-exempt volume to the FINRA numerator, produces a
different population or value.

The query pins full common-date coverage, ratio-of-sums aggregation, absolute
odd-lot-volume cohort selection, short-only FINRA numerator and tie breaks, so

Compare later bank outcomes by starting securities concentration.

The case forms a survivor panel at two year-end dates, records the coincident
ten-year par-yield move, and assigns equal-frequency fifths by each bank's
starting securities-to-assets share with certificate tie-breaking. Later turns
compare margin, deposit, book-equity and cumulative-income outcomes across those

The design is descriptive. Total securities do not identify accounting
classification, duration, purchase date or unrealized gains and losses. Book
equity changes combine earnings with distributions, capital actions, other
comprehensive income and other balance-sheet changes, none of which these fields
decompose. Positive cumulative earnings alongside lower ending equity establishes
only a negative net contribution from all non-earnings changes.

The survivor requirement omits banks that failed or merged, group comparisons do
not control for business model or other confounders, and a large-bank restriction
does not turn the result into a causal estimate. Correlations and tail-group
medians are different descriptive summaries and need not convey the same pattern.

This is a hard baseline case. Numeric validation uses the shared rounding
tolerance; counts match exactly.

later date, to sorting on the securities amount rather than its share of assets, to
using group means rather than medians, to differencing the two group medians rather

naming: the median is not linear, so the lowest group's margin change is 0.1901
percentage points as the median of per-bank changes and 0.134534 as the difference of
the two medians, and the highest group's is 0.0551 against 0.097894. Reporting both
group medians and then subtracting them is the natural reading of a loose phrasing, so
the query now states that the change is taken per bank first. Every one of these
choices is pinned by the query, making them robustness comparisons rather than hidden

docstring:
Turn cumulative bank income into a quarter, and see which ratios survive it.

Bank income statements in the regulatory files are reported year to date. A figure
dated 2024-09-30 covers nine months, not three, and the only way to a quarter is to
subtract the previous quarter's cumulative figure within the same year, with the
first quarter needing no subtraction at all.

Across the 163 banks holding more than 10 billion USD at the 2024-09-30 report date,
followed through the four 2024 dates, the cumulative net interest income divided by
the same panel's own quarterly income comes to 1.0000 at the first date, 2.0047 at
the second, 2.9517 at the third and 3.9125 at the fourth. The multiple is the
quarter number, a little under it because later quarters were larger. At the third
date the panel reports 435.8897 billion USD cumulative against 147.6760 billion
earned in the quarter, and its largest member reports 71.1180 billion against
24.1350, a multiple of 2.9467.

What the convention does to a ratio depends on what is underneath it. A ratio of a
flow to a stock inherits the period: net income over assets at the third date is a
nine-month return, and its median of 0.7334 percent is exactly 0.7500 of the 0.9779
percent that the same income annualized returns, the annualization factor and
nothing else. The denominator is a separate choice again. Bridging the panel to
reported risk-weighted assets through the branch file leaves 158 banks whose
risk-weighted assets are a median 0.7320 of total assets, so the same annualized
income measured against them returns a median 1.3918 percent, 0.4139 points above
the figure measured against assets.

A ratio of one flow to another does not inherit the period, because the factor
appears above and below and cancels. The efficiency ratio needs no annualization at
all. It is still not the same number: computed from cumulative flows it is the
year-to-date average across quarters whose mix differs, not the latest quarter. On
the 156 banks whose revenue base is positive on both bases the cumulative reading
has a median of 58.9811 percent against 57.8794 from the quarter alone, a median
absolute gap of 1.7819 points, and 25 of them differ by more than 5.

Measured rejected alternatives, from the `bank_ytd_flow_derivation` comparison, include annualizing the third quarter by four rather than by four thirds, setting
the panel at 1 billion USD of assets rather than 10, retaining banks whose
quarterly revenue base is not positive, substituting risk-weighted assets for
total assets, and counting a wide efficiency gap from 3 points rather than 5.
The query explicitly fixes each convention needed for the scored calculation, so
these probes test instruction following and reconciliation rather than a live
hidden-method trap. This is therefore a hard baseline case.

Knowledge made explicit in the query: regulatory income statements accumulate
within a year, a partial-year flow is annualized by four over the quarter number,
returns on total and risk-weighted assets use different denominators, and a ratio
of two flows from the same period requires no separate annualization factor.

Boundaries: this is one panel at one date, and the multiples depend on how income
was distributed across the quarters of that year rather than being fixed by the
convention. Differencing assumes the cumulative series is internally consistent; a
restatement inside the year would show up as a distorted quarter. The efficiency
ratio is unstable where a bank's quarterly revenue base is small, and the largest
gap in this panel reaches 139.5809 points on that account.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for
N requested decimals; counts and bank names match exactly.

docstring:
Separate a BDC's funded loan maturities from unfunded commitment marks.

The frozen BlackRock Private Credit Fund filing has 342 debt rows with positive
principal, positive reported fair value and maturity. One further positive-
principal row lacks fair value and is excluded, not valued at zero. The funded
cohort first crosses a 10% cumulative-principal maturity screen at 2028-09-30.
There are 55 zero-principal negative-fair-value rows; six mature by that same
date. The filing says negative balances represent unfunded commitments acquired
or valued at a discount, but their marks do not report undrawn notional.

Measured alternative readings: counting the one positive-principal row with
missing fair value would give 343 funded rows and USD 2,092.143582 million of
principal instead of 342 and USD 2,091.012197 million. Dropping all negative
marks would overstate the signed schedule fair value by USD 2.317280 million.
Adding schedule fair value to reported cash gives USD 2,116.228490 million,
USD 26.073568 million below total assets because other asset lines exist.
This is a baseline: the query states the mutually exclusive row cohorts and
asks for their distinct financial meanings.

docstring:
A BDC cross-section assembled by fiscal-period label mixes reporting dates.

Business development companies do not share a fiscal calendar. Of the 167 filers
in this filing index, 22 close their year somewhere other than 31 December, so
the label "fiscal 2024 Q3" is attached to period ends from 2023-11-30 through
2024-09-30. An analyst who groups by the label rather than by the calendar
period end builds a cross-section whose marks are up to 305 days apart, and for
floating-rate loan books that spans a move in the front-end rate: overnight SOFR
was 5.33% at the earliest of those dates and 4.96% at the latest, the September
2024 cut falling in between.

Three conventions the query states. Only the first, and the negative half of
the second, change a reported number; the rest are stated so that the answer is
well posed rather than because a competing reading would score differently.
Measured alternatives: dropping a whole accession on one absent mark gives
447,864.528 rather than 1,287,095.147 USD millions; excluding negative marks
gives 1,299,091.220. Excluding zero marks, and retaining the earliest rather
than the latest filed accession, both reproduce every reported output exactly,
the latter because the amendment restates an identical 1,132-row schedule:

1. ``fair_value_usd`` is absent on 5.79% of the rows in this label's filings,
   touching 91 of the 135 accessions that carry schedule rows. Dropping a whole
   accession on one missing mark would discard two thirds of the cross-section,
   so a missing mark contributes nothing and the surviving total is a reported
   floor rather than a portfolio valuation.
2. 6,082 rows carry a negative fair value and 5,616 carry zero. Both are real
   reported marks, so neither is filtered.
3. One filer appears twice under the label, a 10-Q and the 10-Q/A filed the next
   day. Keeping the latest filed accession per filer is what makes the
   cross-section one row per filer.

Only 135 of the 163 filers carrying the label have rows in the investment
schedule, so the share counts and the value totals rest on different
denominators; both are reported rather than blended.

docstring:
Branch from a real-EER stress screen into a disciplined credit time-series model.

The case maps USD, EUR and JPY denominations to the corresponding BIS broad real
effective exchange-rate reference areas.  It selects the currency with the
largest absolute 2019-Q1-to-2025-Q4 real-EER change, then carries that currency
into the BIS EME non-bank credit decomposition.

An Engle--Granger residual ADF diagnostic is estimated on 2000-Q1--2022-Q4.  The
public contract uses a fixed finite-sample critical boundary.  The frozen JPY
sample does not reject a unit root, so the live branch estimates a stationary
first-difference ARDL rather than claiming an error-correction equilibrium.  The
terminal 2023--2025 rolling ex-post conditional-prediction exercise uses the
realized contemporaneous loan change, compares the fitted relation with a
no-change benchmark, and overlays the selected quarter's real-EER move.  It is
not an ex-ante forecast comparison.  Normal-equation
moments and component-versus-total credit identities are explicit invariants.

The `bis_currency_cointegration` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to screening on
the nominal rather than the real effective exchange rate, to forcing an
error-correction specification instead of letting the residual diagnostic choose the
branch, and to benchmarking the conditional forecast against the training-mean change
rather than no change. The branch rule is the one worth naming: the frozen JPY residual
gives an ADF t statistic of -1.345669, which does not reject a unit root, so forcing
error correction would report an adjustment coefficient the data does not support. The
query fixes all three, so these are robustness comparisons rather than hidden answer
paths.

docstring:
Estimate a generalized-FEVD connectedness network for EME credit and stress.

The three credit series are BIS total credit, loans plus debt securities from all
lenders, to non-bank borrowers in emerging-market and developing economies, one series
each for dollar-, euro- and yen-denominated lending, alongside the quarterly mean OFR
Financial Stress Index. A generalized forecast-error variance decomposition asks how
much of each series' forecast error is explained by shocks to the others without
imposing the ordering a Cholesky decomposition needs, which matters because there is no
defensible causal ordering between three funding currencies and a stress index.

On the VAR(2) estimated over 2001-Q1 through 2024-Q4 the decomposition keeps 78.8363
percent of the dollar forecast error at home and 91.1030 percent of the yen, and total
connectedness across the four nodes is 18.1924 percent. Dollar credit growth is the net
transmitter at 7.3174 percentage points; the euro is the largest net receiver at
-17.6226, taking 22.2167 percent of its variance from the others while sending 4.5941.
The largest single directed edge runs from the stress index into dollar credit growth at
14.3627 percent rather than between two currencies.

Each decomposition row is normalized to sum to 100 percent, and the reported row-sum
residual is zero at the precision the output is scored to. The innovation covariance condition number is 10.9757, so the
generalized weights are not read off a near-singular matrix, and the maximum OLS normal
moment is zero at the scored precision.

The `bis_var_connectedness` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to differencing the
published levels rather than using quarter-over-quarter log growth, to the VAR lag
order, and to the decomposition horizon. The query fixes all three, so these are
robustness comparisons rather than hidden answer paths.

Boundaries: a generalized decomposition is invariant to variable ordering but is not a
causal identification, and the shares describe this estimated system over this sample
rather than a structural transmission mechanism. The impulse responses are generalized
rather than orthogonalized, so they are not the effect of one shock holding the other
series fixed. Credit is measured at quarter-end in nominal terms, so valuation effects
from exchange-rate moves are inside the growth series rather than separated from it.

docstring:
Compare repurchases, stock compensation and subsequent share-count outcomes.

Operating cash flow adds back share-based compensation because it is noncash.
That does not make the resulting cash unavailable for distribution; the cost to
existing owners can instead arrive through dilution. Operating cash flow less
reported PP&E purchases includes growth as well as maintenance investment and
does not by itself measure sustainable distributable cash.
Across the 1,251 annual filings in this window, share-based compensation is
176.353726 USD billions against 1585.787171 of operating cash flow, a median
8.1852% of a filer's own operating cash flow.

The case turns on an association that can be checked. Of the
1,039 filers reporting a repurchase, 352 repurchase less than they expensed in
stock compensation. Among the 989 with
a prior-year annual filing to compare against, 72.5076% of the ones repurchasing
below their compensation saw weighted-average basic shares rise, against
19.7568% of the ones repurchasing at or above it. The first group's median
share count rose 0.7811%; the second group's fell.

Three conventions the data forces:

1. ``PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment``, ``PaymentsForRepurchaseOf
   CommonStock`` and ``ShareBasedCompensation`` are outflow and expense
   concepts can carry unexpected negative values. A reversal, recovery,
   presentation choice or data fault may explain one; these data do not
   distinguish them. Eight of the 1,259 filers tagging all four are dropped
   by the stated sign screen rather than sign-flipped: 1 capital expenditure, 3 repurchases and
   5 compensation amounts are negative, nine flags across eight filers because
   one trips two. Reading them as positives would substitute unreported amounts.
2. The prior-year filing is the latest original annual report 300 to 430 days
   before the current one, found by that distance rather than by a calendar
   year: three 52/53-week filers closed their preceding year on 2024-01-01 or
   2024-01-02, 364 days earlier, and a search of 2023 period ends finds no
   prior year for them. The window keeps out the one filer whose nearest
   earlier report sits 731 days back, so a year-over-year share count stays a
   year.
3. ``PaymentsOfDividends`` carries no total on its own. Only 825 of the 5,524
   annual filings tag it, most filers using a variant concept this table does
   not carry, so the dividends are taken from the separate fact file instead:
   of the 122 eligible filers recording a selected annual dividend fact there,
   including zero-valued facts, the single
   concept would find 49. Two conventions hold that total together. An
   aggregate supersedes its own components, without which one filer's payment
   is counted twice and the total reads 291.380830 rather than 281.566830 USD
   billions; and a year is taken as first filed, one filer otherwise carrying
   782,000,000 restated a year later in place of the 782,048,000 it first
   reported. The aggregate and common/ordinary/preferred fallback do not
   have a uniform recipient scope; this is a selected-concept screen rather
   than a homogeneous parent-shareholder payout total.

Both medians are taken with linear interpolation, which the query states. It
binds for the compensation share, whose group has an even count with two
differing middle values: 8.1311 or 8.2392 against the reported 8.1852 under the
lower or the upper middle value. The below-compensation group has an odd count,
331, so its median share-count change is one filer's and no convention moves it.

Every selection above changes a reported number. The one that does not is the
guard requiring a positive prior share count, which no filer trips; it stays in
the code because it is a divisor and is left out of the query because a solver
would spend a step on a condition that never binds.

The repurchase total is what filers tagged, not an audited figure. 177 of the
repurchasers spend more than their own operating cash flow, which can reflect
financing, other cash sources or a tagging mismatch: NetApp reports
15,600,000,000 against operating cash flow of 1,685,000,000, and its series
across 2019 to 2025 runs 11.7, 13.1, 13.3, 13.9, 0.85, 15.6 and 16.8 billions,
a cumulative program total sitting in an annual field in every year but one.
The screen is reported for what it is and no threshold is applied to repair it.

docstring:
The cash flow statement reconciles cash including restricted cash.

Since the 2016 update to the cash flow standard, the three activity totals and
the effect of exchange rates reconcile the change in cash, cash equivalents
and restricted cash together, not the balance-sheet cash line alone. A check
written against that cash line fails for any filer that holds restricted cash,
however clean its statement is.

Across the 3,642 annual reports for 2024 that carry all three activity totals
and a cash balance at both ends of the year, the three totals reproduce the
change in the cash line to within three dollars for 1,162. The other 2,480 are not
all errors. Among the filers that also appear in the fact set covering the
largest filers, reading both balances from the same annual report and adding
the effect of exchange rates, the reconciliation against cash including
restricted cash closes for 354 of 402, and against the cash line alone for 93
of 308. 183 of the 284 filers that report both closing balances hold restricted
cash, and 185 report an effect of exchange rates other than zero.

Eight conventions the query states because each moves an output:

1. The opening balance in the fact-set comparison is the comparative column of
   the same annual report. The prior year's own report can differ where the
   figure was later revised: of the 393 filers carrying both combined opening
   figures, 16 differ, and among those the reconciliation closes for 10 from
   the comparative figure and for 1 from the prior report's own. On the cash
   line alone 13 of 300 differ, and reconciling the cash line from the prior
   report instead closes 88 of 300 rather than 93 of 308.
2. An effect of exchange rates the filer does not report is taken as zero. Of
   the 402 filers checkable on the inclusive balance, 223 report none and 190
   of those close on that reading; dropping them instead leaves 179 checkable
   and 164 closing.
3. A reconciliation closes within three dollars. It rests on five figures,
   three totals and two balances, each rounded to the dollar at worst, so a
   correct statement can miss by up to two and a half. The threshold is not a
   boundary any figure sits on: five first-turn reports miss by exactly one
   dollar and the next smallest miss is six, while in the fact-set comparison
   the smallest miss that is not zero is 27,000 dollars. A threshold of one
   dollar would sit exactly on those five and read 1,162 or 1,157 according
   to whether the comparison is strict.
4. The combined balance and its exchange effect are both the plain lines,
   not the variants that add cash held in disposal groups and discontinued
   operations. 38 filers report the exchange effect only on the variant line,
   all of them nonzero; the plain reading takes their plain effect as zero.
   Taking the effect from whichever line carries it instead reads 374 of 402
   closing on the combined balance, 103 of 308 on the cash line alone and 223
   nonzero effects. Using the variant family throughout, balances and effect
   alike, wherever a filer reports it reads 404 of 430. The plain family is
   the one every filer in the comparison can be checked against the same way.
   The balance variant on its own: 41 of the filers in
   the comparison report that variant and 24 report it without the plain
   total; preferring it wherever it appears gives 426 checkable and 367
   closing rather than 402 and 354, a lower closure rate, so the variant is
   stated out rather than chosen.
   The cash-only balance is likewise the same line the first turn reads.
   Among the filers in the comparison that do not report it, 49 report a
   bank's cash and amounts due from banks and 18 report cash excluding
   equivalents; substituting either would change who is checkable.
5. A report filed jointly under two filers, a parent and its operating
   partnership, is counted once. Three such reports appear in 2024 and two of
   them enter the first-turn population, so counting by filer would read
   3,644 rather than 3,642 and credit the same statement twice.
6. The first-turn opening balance comes from the filer's own report for a
   fiscal year ending between 350 and 380 days earlier, which leaves out 11
   filers whose fiscal year moved; admitting them gives 3,653 reports and the
   same 1,162 that close.
7. The second turn returns to every 2024 report, not only the first turn's
   final population. Carrying the first turn's population forward instead
   leaves 277 checkable on the combined balance, 238 closing and 147 nonzero
   exchange effects, rather than 402, 354 and 185.
8. Amendments are outside the population. Admitting them, the later filing
   then winning the tie, reads 3,615 filers and 1,162 falls to 1,161.

docstring:
Two federal responses to the same flood, over two different sets of counties.

A disaster declaration designates counties one at a time and names which
programmes each one gets. Flood insurance pays policyholders wherever they are.
The two footprints are not the same and do not line up the way a county count
suggests. Of the 1,193 counties with a 2024 flood claim, 811 were never inside
a major disaster declaration for a water-driven incident that year, so by count
most insured loss sits outside the declaration system; those 811 counties paid
247.0510 USD millions against 8798.2578 in total, so by money almost none of it
does.

Four things about the declaration file decide the population:

1. ``individual_assistance_declared`` is false on every one of the 19,167 rows
   in this extract, so a screen written against it returns nothing. The live
   household flag is ``individuals_households_program_declared``, true on 368
   of the rows here. Both names describe household aid and only one carries
   information.
2. Emergency declarations never authorise household assistance: all 368 rows
   carrying that flag are major disaster declarations, and none of the 813
   emergency rows do. Counting designations without separating the declaration
   type puts 877 counties in the population where 630 can receive the
   programme being measured.
3. A code ending 000 is a tribal or statewide designation rather than a county,
   and the 21 such rows here name areas as distinct as the Eastern Band of
   Cherokee Indians and the St. Regis Mohawk Indian Reservation while sharing
   six state-level codes between them. Keeping them would put 1,646 rows and
   883 counties in the population and would count several tribal areas as one
   place. The claim side drops the same codes, so the two sides are screened
   alike.
4. A county is designated once per disaster, and 149 of them are designated
   under more than one 2024 disaster. A county counts as having the household
   programme if any of its designations carries the flag, which is what makes
   the county rather than the designation the unit.

Two conventions on the claim side. Payments are the signed net building,
contents and increased-cost-of-compliance amounts: the gross columns are
absent on 5,029 of these rows while the net columns are complete, and gross
gives 8801.1170 against the reported 8798.2578, while dropping the
compliance component gives 8787.3735. And 27 claims carry a negative net
payment and 16,444 a zero; both are reported outcomes of a claim and neither
is filtered.

The incident window is the incident begin date rather than the declaration
date, which follows the event instead of the paperwork and moves the row count

Optimize an exponential-omega/stationary-softmax parameterization by L-BFGS-B to a 0.0000000000001 relative objective tolerance and 3000-iteration cap. Both starts use the preliminary OLS mean coefficients; their omega values are 0.03 and 0.08 times the initial variance and their shock/lagged-variance pairs are respectively (0.0158603637364903, 0.8659465188651376) and (0.0899405425972101, 0.6645757148190471). Choose the converged finite fit with greater likelihood, breaking an exact tie lexicographically; fail if neither converges. Report the mean coefficients, variance parameters, persistence, implied unconditional volatility, maximized log likelihood, and the maximum absolute unscaled squared-percentage recursion residual over observations after the initializer. Also report the minimum fitted-minus-perturbed log-likelihood loss when, holding the fitted mean and initializer fixed, omega is multiplied by 1.05 or 0.95, alpha by 1.01, or beta by 0.999 one at a time. docstring:
Oil-conditioned Gaussian GARCH tail diagnostics for energy-industry returns.

Energy-industry excess returns are heteroskedastic and partly driven by oil, so a
constant-variance value-at-risk understates risk in turbulent months and overstates it
in calm ones. The case fits a GARCH(1,1) whose conditional mean carries the
contemporaneous WTI log return, then asks whether the resulting conditional tail
forecasts are calibrated out of sample.

The 2018-2022 fit gives an oil mean beta of 0.43729 and a variance recursion with
alpha 0.13192 and beta 0.85231, so persistence is 0.984227 and unconditional
volatility 2.033 percent per day. The training log likelihood is -2347.796258 and
the variance recursion reproduces itself exactly, with a maximum recursion residual of
0.0.

Over the 745 held-out days the one-percent conditional Gaussian bound is breached 7
times against 7.45 expected, a 0.939597 percent rate, and the Kupiec unconditional
coverage test cannot reject calibration with a likelihood ratio of 0.0280 and a
p-value of 0.8671. The interesting result is what happens inside the stress
subsample: on the ten highest-OFR-stress days conditional volatility nearly doubles to
2.1358 percent against 1.195352 on the other days, yet not one of those days breaches
the bound and the realized mean loss is -0.097 percent, a gain. Average expected
shortfall on those days is 5.8522 percent, so the model overshoots realized loss by
5.9492 percentage points. A model that passes an unconditional coverage test can still
be badly calibrated on the subsample a risk manager cares about.

The query fixes the estimator completely, including the two-start L-BFGS-B optimizer,
its relative objective tolerance and iteration cap, the parameterization and the
starting values, so the fitted parameters are determined by the question rather than by
the solver a model happens to reach for. The five parameters are pinned at 5 decimals
and every downstream quantity is computed from unrounded parameters.

Precision is set by what the optimizer reproduces, not by what the arithmetic could
print. Running this module on two machines that differ only in their BLAS moves the
fitted alpha in its sixth decimal, and the quantities derived from it move further:
persistence by 2e-8, implied unconditional volatility by 2e-6 and the stress-tail
Gaussian ES by 2e-6. Persistence, the perturbation loss, the conditional Gaussian VaR
and ES averages, and the three stress-tail volatility and ES figures are therefore
pinned at 4 to 6 decimals -- each with at least twenty-five times the observed
cross-machine spread in its tolerance -- so the shared rounding-boundary tolerance
absorbs solver dispersion between conforming implementations without admitting a second
estimator.

The `energy_garch_ofr_tail` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to using simple rather
than log WTI returns, to the tail probability, and to the number of stress days in the
subsample. The query fixes all three, so these are robustness comparisons rather than
hidden answer paths.

Boundaries: a Gaussian innovation is assumed rather than tested, so the tail forecasts
inherit that assumption and expected shortfall in particular is sensitive to it. The

# Kupiec unconditional coverage LR test
p = 0.01
n = n_test
x_breach = conditional_var_breach_count

Report how many securities are recorded on at least half the window's settlement dates. Explain what recurrence on half the window's dates selects for.
docstring:
Three measures of the same settlement failures, and three different answers.

The trap is the denominator of an average, and it fires in the first turn.
A security's undelivered balance is a level that stands on every settlement date,
including the dates the file leaves it out, because leaving it out means the
balance was nil. The average balance per settlement date therefore divides the
summed balance by the 126 dates in the window. Grouping by symbol and calling the
frame's own mean instead divides by the number of dates the security happens to
appear on, which is the pandas default and reads as the same sentence in code.

The window's settlement-date count is reported in the last turn rather than the
first, so the first turn never hands the denominator over as a prior result. The
reader still has to decide that a date the file omits is a date with no
undelivered balance, which is the judgement the query leaves open.

Measured. The correct leader averages 3,226,336.2778 shares per settlement date
and stands 17.4323 percent above the runner-up. The default mean returns
3,946,780.3010 shares for that same security, 22.3301 percent high, and collapses
the margin to 1.4707 percent because the runner-up gains more from the shorter
denominator than the leader does. The wrong path therefore changes two of the
first turn's outputs, the average and the margin, and leaves the leading symbol
correct -- the model reaches the right security and reports the wrong size of its
problem. At four requested decimals the rounding-boundary tolerance is 0.00006
shares against a separation of 720,444.0232, so neither wrong figure can enter
the accepted band. Turns two through four rest on summed balances and summed
valued balances, which the denominator never touches, so the path stays confined
to the first turn.

The second measure is the case's financial point. Valuing each balance at its own
date's reported price moves the lead from a low-priced satellite-radio issuer to
an index fund: 10,295.9579 million USD against a runner-up 16.8980 percent
behind, while the share-count leader falls to fifteenth. Counting shares ranks
securities by how many are cheap; counting dollars ranks them by how much capital
is undelivered, and a failure in a fund share is generally an artifact of
creation and redemption rather than a short position. The third measure shows
that the obvious way to normalise either of them is unavailable where it matters:
511 of the 3,694 cohort securities carry a reported share count and only 4 of the
twenty largest by valued balance do, so the carrying securities hold 35.6545
percent of the cohort's balance but only 18.5381 percent of its valued balance.
Coverage falls as exposure rises, because an exchange-traded fund files no
periodic report carrying a share count.

Two conventions the query leaves out because they change nothing. Whether the
share-count search honours amendments as well as original periodic filings moves
the qualifying ticker universe from 3,824 to 3,828 and leaves all four of the
third turn's outputs identical. Choosing a single filing per ticker is likewise
idle: the case asks whether a count exists, never what it is. Only the filing
cutoff is load bearing, and it excludes 199 tickers whose first reported count
arrives after the window.

Measured alternative readings, all pinned by the query. Dropping the dates that
report no price before summing balances leaves the leader and its average
unchanged but moves the margin to 74.8327 percent, because a fifth of the
window's failed shares -- 8,101 rows, 1.2574 percent of the window, carrying
20.2522 percent of its shares -- sit on rows with no price; the query says a
balance stands whether or not a price is reported, and the module values a
balance only where a price exists. Moving the recurrence floor to a quarter or
three quarters of the dates changes the cohort to 8,580 or 944 securities and
leaves both leaders where they are, so the floor is pinned for the count it
reports rather than for the ranking.

No rank the case uses is tied: the average-balance leader stands 17.4323 percent
above the runner-up, the valued leader 16.8980 percent, and the twentieth valued
security 6.6970 percent above the twenty-first.

The final turn spans a shortened settlement cycle. Average balances rose from
78,554,279.1452 to 93,658,451.4444 shares per date across the two halves of 2024,
which hold 124 and 126 settlement dates, a ratio of 1.1923, which runs opposite to the expectation that a shorter cycle
leaves less room for delivery to fail. Nothing in these two sources separates
that move from issuance, volume or composition, and the required claim asks the
response to say so.

docstring:
A financed Treasury floating-rate note, and the credit line it breaches.

A March 2025 reopening of the two-year floating-rate note is bought at auction
and funded entirely at realized SOFR. The note pays a quarterly coupon indexed to
the thirteen-week bill; the loan accrues daily. Each coupon is swept into
repayment on arrival, so the loan drifts with the difference between the two
rates rather than with either one, and the position needs no view on direction to
be worth measuring.

The identification is a data contract before it is a calculation. The auction
table does not carry a floating-rate security type: these notes are recorded as
Notes, and the `floating_rate` flag is what separates them. Exactly one such
auction settles in March 2025.

The coupon convention decides the answer. The index is the high discount rate of
the most recent thirteen-week bill auction, converted to an ACT/360 money-market
yield over that bill's own term, and it is frozen for the final two business days
before each payment date. Without the freeze the first coupon comes to 1.075643
per 100 rather than 1.075714, which is 0.71 dollars on a million of face and more
than ten times the tolerance this case scores at, so the query pins it.

Cash amounts are reported in USD thousands to five decimals rather than four.
A coupon settled to the cent is 10,757.14 dollars, which is 10.75714 thousand: a
four-decimal contract would leave 10.7571 and the incorrectly rounded 10.7572
both inside the shared tolerance, and a band wider than the value's own precision
is exactly what the validator contract forbids.

The financing leg pins its own conventions: a SOFR observation date defines a
business day, one simple factor covers each interval including the non-business
days inside it, and factors compound between intervals.

Rejected alternative conventions, each measured against the pinned reading:

- Freezing nothing before the payment date gives a first coupon of 10,756.43
  against 10,757.14, and a second post-payment loan balance of 999,756.51.
- Taking the index from the bill's issue date rather than its auction date, so a
  rate applies three days later than it does, gives a first coupon of 10,754.58.
- Converting the bill's discount rate over a fixed 91 days rather than its own
  term gives 10,757.04.
- Financing only the clean price and leaving the accrued interest unfunded starts
  the loan 6,770.46 lower and never reaches the credit limit at all, so the final
  turn reports no contribution.

docstring:
Two ways to misread a fund's redemption record, and a market that settles both.

Form N-PORT gives each filing three months of share sales, share redemptions and
investment gains. Neither the months nor the redemptions read the way a frame
suggests, and this case is built on both.

The first trap is the sign, and it fires in the first turn. A redemption is an
amount paid out, but the filer chooses how to sign the field: 183,280 of the
874,476 redemption observations on this file are negative, 66,327 of the 290,709
retained filings carry at least one negative month, they come from 655 registrants,
and 4,416 series report both signs at different times. Adding the column up
therefore returns 35,417.3573 billion dollars against the 53,220.9308 actually
redeemed, understating the total by 33.4522 percent. At four requested decimals
the rounding-boundary tolerance is 0.00006 billion dollars, so the naive figure
cannot enter the accepted band.

The second trap is the calendar, and it fires in the second turn. The three
reported months are the first, second and third months of the reporting period,
so the third is the month the period ends in and the first is two months earlier.
Reading the first as the most recent inverts the order. On the lowest-return month
in the covered window the inverted reading returns 888.2351 billion dollars
redeemed against 1,552.7608, low by 42.7964 percent, and taking both wrong paths
at once returns 396.2804. The inversion is not a coverage artifact: both readings
draw on the same 11,597 filings and differ only in which of the three columns they
take.

The market settles the calendar without the query having to. Each reported month's
investment gain as a fraction of net assets carries a Spearman rank correlation of
0.6696 with the market return two months before the period end for the first
month, 0.7105 one month before for the second, and 0.6716 with the period-end
month for the third. Every off-diagonal entry of that table lies between -0.1227
and 0.0462. Tied values take their average rank, which the query states because the tie
handling moves the answer: minimum, maximum, first-seen and dense ranking return
0.6691, 0.6701, 0.6694 and 0.6653 against 0.6696, all outside a tolerance of
0.00006. Ties dominate one side of the pairing, since the market column carries
only 75 distinct values across 290,709 observations.

The rank statistic is used because Pearson is not robust here: 538 of
872,130 gain observations exceed half of net assets in absolute value, and leaving
them in collapses the diagonal from roughly 0.65 to 0.02, which would make the
diagnostic an artifact of a trimming threshold rather than a fact about the file.

The financial content is what the corrected record then shows. The lowest-return
month in the window is March 2020 at -13.1824 percent, ahead of the runner-up by
3.7683 percentage points, and it is the month of the dash for cash. Corrected, the
filings covering it record 1,552.7608 billion dollars redeemed against sales that
leave a net of -392.7647 billion; the sign-naive path reports a positive net
instead, which contradicts the episode. Within the period, one month carries a
median 0.4728 of the three-month redemption total, so quarterly aggregation halves
the visible stress; 2,431 filings redeemed more than a tenth of net assets in that
single month, and 503 of them -- 20.69 percent -- still show sales above
redemptions across the whole period, so a reader working at period grain sees an
inflow where a month of run-scale redemption happened.

A third rule earns its words too. Nineteen series moved their reporting cycle and
report the selected month in two periods at once; both filings state the same
month figure but rest on different period ends, so entering both would count
1,552.7608 billion dollars as 1,553.6928 and shift the net by 0.3656 billion,
against a tolerance of 0.00006. The series is counted once, keeping the filing
whose period ends earliest and so whose net assets are measured closest to the
month. Across the file 633 of 871,491 series-months are covered twice.

Two population rules earn their words in the query. 16,620 filings report no
series identifier, from 1,196 registrants of which only 10 also file with one, so
a grouping that keys on the identifier discards them by default; the query states
the exclusion instead of leaving it to that default. 15,673 of those filings do
carry a series name, so the identifier is what is absent rather than the fund. The
registrants visible in the excluded set are unit investment trusts and standalone
closed-end funds -- SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, General American Investors, Adams
Diversified Equity, AllianceBernstein Global High Income -- whose shares are not
redeemed for cash by the shareholder the way an open-end fund's are; the case
records that composition without asserting it of all 1,196. The exclusion is not
immaterial: those filings report a further 198.6938 billion dollars redeemed in
the selected month, 12.80 percent on top of the figure this case reports, so the
month total is the series-identified population's and not the whole file's.
And the surviving filing is taken whole: a column-wise retention carries a value
forward from the superseded filing wherever the successor leaves that column
empty, which spliced one filing here and moved the sold total by 0.0015 billion
dollars against a tolerance of 0.00006.

Sales are summed as reported. The sign of the sales field is not the filer's
convention the way the redemption field's is: 486 of the retained sales
observations are negative, in 465 filings, and 290 of the 293 series behind them
report positive sales in other filings; a negative month typically cancels the
one before it (5,233.44 sold, then -5,233.44). It reverses a sale, so taking its
magnitude would count the reversal as a further sale and move the sold total from
54,502.1314 to 54,512.7889 billion dollars. Of the other outputs only the
month's net flow reads it, and it moves by 0.0000025 billion, inside its tolerance.

Fragility of the anchors. The lowest-return month leads by 3.7683 percentage
points and the largest single filing, 69.0542 billion dollars, leads the runner-up
by 88.9458 percent, so neither selection is close. The retained-filing rule is not
idle either: 4,614 series-period pairs carry more than one filing and 88 of those
pairs disagree on a reported redemption.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for N
requested decimals; counts, the offset and the date match exactly.

docstring:
A field that cannot be averaged, and a denial reason that names it.

The mortgage disclosure file reports debt-to-income three different ways in one
column. Between 36 and 49 percent it reports the exact integer; outside that
band it reports a range, ``<20%`` through ``>60%``; and where the ratio is not
collected it reports ``NA`` or ``Exempt``. Twenty-one values, of which nineteen
sit on a scale and two do not. 4,320,765 of the 12,043,028 records carry one of
the two that do not, so a third of the file cannot be placed on the axis at
all, and no mean of this column is defined: ``>60%`` has no number behind it
and ``30%-<36%`` is not 33.

``Exempt`` is not a missing value. It marks a filer using the partial reporting
exemption, which is open to smaller insured depositories and credit unions, and
the institution file shows it: of the 12,043,028 records, the 2,999,048 filed
by a lender the file maps to a deposit-insurance certificate carry ``Exempt``
on 5.2955% against 1.3361% for the rest. The code is about who filed, not
about the borrower.

The denial reason points at the same field. 668,880 records are denied with
debt-to-income named as the first reason, and the reported ratio agrees with
that most of the time: 545,342 of them sit at 50% or above, and the class at
the median of the denied records is ``>60%`` against ``41`` across every
orderable record in the file. It does not always agree. 25,287 of the records

judgement against a programme's own limit, while the field records a ratio
computed under the reporting rules, and one can fail where the other looks fine.

Three conventions the data forces:

   way against the 41 the scale gives.
2. The median is the first class whose cumulative count reaches half the

the other cases drawing on this file name their codes the same way, so the
alternative would be a test of a codebook rather than of the column.

   of this data.

applications whose ratio the filer was not required to report, and dropping
them would shrink the denominator of every share in this case.

A stressed mortgage-pool acquisition whose FHA comparison must not replace the pool being bought.

The acquisition pool is built from 2024 Florida conventional first-lien purchase
originations, re-underwritten as hypothetical level-payment loans and stressed through a
joint payment-burden and collateral default test. An FHA pool is then evaluated as a
comparison and put through a severe alternative, after which the quote and the leveraged
purchase return to the conventional pool under its base underwriting case. The case
measures whether that original state survives two intervening analyses.

Rejected alternative conventions, each measured against the pinned reading:

- Quoting the FHA comparison instead of the acquisition pool moves the bid from 99.1857
  to 93.5013 per 100 and turns the leveraged equity return from 9.1488 to -6.9655
  percent.
- Carrying the severe FHA shock into the acquisition quote gives a bid of 93.8739 and a
  return of -5.8247 percent.
- Leaving property values unindexed instead of applying the 2023Q4-2024Q4 FHFA growth
  raises the base terminal credit loss from 974.1388 to 1,085.1055 million.
- A 240-month term instead of 360 raises the aggregate monthly payment from 237.6023 to
  279.1054 million and changes 11 of the 14 outputs.

docstring:
Predict a crash from estimated betas, then measure how badly the betas held.

A market beta is the multiplier a linear factor model puts on a systematic move, so
it is the natural instrument for asking what a market decline does to a portfolio.
Estimated on the 1,253 trading days from 2015 through 2019 on which the industry
returns, the research factors and the daily oil price all report, the ten
value-weighted industry portfolios span a wide range: technology at 1.1750 and
utilities at 0.4311.

Between 2020-02-19 and 2020-03-23, 24 trading days, the market excess return summed
to -38.3400 percent. Because the model is linear in daily returns, the prediction it
implies is the intercept times the number of days plus beta times that sum, and the
outcome it should be compared with is the same arithmetic sum of daily excess
returns rather than a compounded return. On that footing the predictions miss by a
mean absolute 12.9895 percentage points, and 7 of the 10 industries fell further
than their beta said they would.

Scaling each industry's estimation-period residual standard deviation to a 24-day
window gives a diagnostic distance for the cumulative residual, and 9 of the 10
industries land more than three such units from their prediction; telecommunications
is at -1.0506. These ratios are not calibrated hypothesis-test probabilities.
Utilities is the sharpest failure: a beta of 0.4311 predicted -16.1914 percent and
it delivered -44.4900, a miss of -28.2986 at -7.7540 standard errors. The low-beta
defensive sector did not defend. Technology missed as far in the other direction,
predicted at -44.5995 and delivering -32.6600, a positive 11.9395 at 6.0525.
Ranking by raw miss and by standard errors does not agree: energy has the largest
miss at -29.4706 but utilities the most extreme one, because energy's residuals were
always wider.

Oil collapsed over the same window from 53.31 to 23.33 dollars a barrel, a fall of
56.2371 percent and a daily sum of -63.9247. Re-estimating each industry on the market and the daily oil
return together, energy carries an oil loading of 0.2731 and its miss narrows from
-29.4706 to -20.0608, a 31.9294 percent numerical reduction in absolute miss.
Utilities carries an oil loading of 0.0161 and its miss barely moves, to -27.7425.
This is a fitted-prediction comparison, not a causal decomposition.

The `industry_beta_crisis` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to geometric
cumulation, omitting the intercept, changing the estimation or crisis window, using
raw rather than excess industry returns, and reporting the widest miss without its
sign after selecting the industry on absolute error. The query fixes the reported
linear-model convention, so these are robustness comparisons rather than hidden
answer paths.

Interpretive boundary: beta describes an estimated average sensitivity in the
chosen period, not a promise about a crisis. The residual scaling is a model-distance
diagnostic, and a linear daily-return prediction is evaluated against an arithmetic
sum on the same basis.

Boundaries: this is one episode, and an episode selected because it was severe.
The standard error used here is the estimation-period residual standard
deviation scaled by the square root of the day count, which treats those
residuals as independent and identically distributed, something a crisis is
precisely the occasion to doubt, and which omits the uncertainty in the fitted
coefficients themselves. That omission is not large but it is not nothing:
adding it inflates the standard errors by a median factor of 1.0433, which
leaves utilities at -7.4319 and energy at -5.7586 but moves health care from
3.0306 to 2.9047 and so takes the count beyond three from 9 to 8. The figures
reported here are distances from the model rather than calibrated probabilities.
The oil test uses a spot price rather than the futures curve the industry
actually hedges on.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for
N requested decimals; counts and industry labels match exactly.

Treating the 1,258 observed scenarios as a uniform discrete population (each equally likely with probability 1/1258, not a sample estimate), the population standard deviation of this constructed daily return series is 1.3912 percentage point

var_desc: Store posterior-relative-to-prior Kullback-Leibler divergence using natural logs, rounded to 4 decimals. Compute from your own unrounded inputs and carried state, not other rounded outputs.
query: Apply Meucci's discrete Entropy Pooling to the carried prior, minimizing posterior-relative-to-prior Kullback-Leibler divergence on the unchanged scenario support. Give full confidence simultaneously to two equality views: the stress event has probability 20 percent, and the portfolio's expected daily simple return is 0.10 percent. Report the divergence using natural logs, the posterior inverse-Herfindahl effective scenario count and posterior daily portfolio volatility. Carry the entire posterior probability law forward and assess how its information content differs from the historical prior.
code:
# KL divergence of posterior relative to prior (natural log), i.e. KL(p_post || p0)
kl = np.sum(p_post * (np.log(p_post) - np.log(p0)))
entropy_divergence = round(float(kl), 4)

# Effective number of scenarios: inverse-Herfindahl of posterior probabilities
herfindahl = np.sum(p_post**2)
eff_scenarios = 1.0 / herfindahl
effective_scenario_count = round(float(eff_scenarios), 4)

# Posterior daily portfolio volatility (population, weighted by posterior probabilities)
post_mean = np.sum(p_post * port_ret)
post_var = np.sum(p_post * (port_ret - post_mean)**2)
post_vol = np.sqrt(post_var)
posterior_daily_volatility_pct = round(float(post_vol), 4)

print("KL divergence (nats):", kl, "->", entropy_divergence)
print("Herfindahl:", herfindahl, "Effective scenarios:", eff_scenarios, "->", effective_scenario_count)
print("Posterior mean check:", post_mean, "Posterior vol:", post_vol, "->", posterior_daily_volatility_pct)

print("\nFor comparison, prior scenario_count:", scenario_count)
print("Prior volatility:", prior_daily_volatility_pct)

# Carry the full posterior law forward alongside the joint prior/support
joint_prior['posterior_prob'] = p_post
posterior_law = joint_prior.copy()

print(posterior_law[['date','ofr_fsi','stress_event','port_ret_pct','posterior_prob']].head())
print()
print("Posterior probability on stress days vs non-stress days (avg):")
print(posterior_law.groupby('stress_event')['posterior_prob'].agg(['mean','sum','count']))

print("\nFinal values:")
print("entropy_divergence:", entropy_divergence)
print("effective_scenario_count:", effective_scenario_count)
print("posterior_daily_volatility_pct:", posterior_daily_volatility_pct)

Build an equal-risk-contribution industry portfolio before an OFR stress peak.

The later current-revised OFR history selects the largest 2019--2025 FSI level.
That date fixes a 504-common-date training sample ending twenty observations
before the peak and a disjoint sixty-date stress window.  The five industries
with the highest training volatility form the carried cohort; no stress-window
return enters selection or estimation.

The nearest active case, ``industry_beta_crisis_prediction_failure``, shares
the Ken French sources and 22 dates in the COVID stress episode.  It tests the
breakdown of pre-crisis single-factor predictions and an oil-factor omission;
this case instead solves a covariance-based risk budget and allocates portfolio
expected shortfall.  The shared event is therefore a portfolio-concentration
watch item, not the case's financial construct or terminal diagnostic.

The case then estimates a decimal-return sample covariance and Fama--French
three-factor loadings.  Equal-risk-contribution weights are the unique positive,
fully invested solution for equal risk budgets.  The canonical implementation
uses cyclic coordinate descent.  An independent damped-Newton implementation in
the case-local tests agrees to machine precision.  Equal portfolio weights are
not equal risk contributions and produce a measured alternative stress result.
The reported maximum contribution-share deviation is pinned at 5 decimals, so the
exact equal-risk-contribution solution reports zero and the shared rounding-boundary
tolerance absorbs the residual any properly converged solver leaves behind.

The final historical expected shortfall uses daily-rebalanced portfolio returns
and the two worst portfolio-return days in the sixty-date window.  Component
contributions are evaluated on exactly those tail dates and add to portfolio ES,
which is the explicit invariant.  The exercise is a retrospective stress test
using current-revised OFR and Ken French files; it is not a real-time trading
strategy, causal attribution or evidence of future performance.

The `industry_erc_stress` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to selecting the cohort
on the stress window rather than the training window, to a population rather than
sample covariance denominator, to allocating equal weight rather than equal risk
contribution, to raw rather than excess factor returns, and to taking the floor rather
than the ceiling of the tail count. The risk-allocation axis is the one worth naming:
equal portfolio weights are not equal risk contributions, and substituting them
produces a measured alternative stress result. The query fixes all five, so these are
robustness comparisons rather than hidden answer paths.

- Dividing residual variance by the observation count instead of the count minus four

proves unique economic-event identity nor establishes the first publication in
every possible source.

docstring:
Beneficial ownership disclosed in Form 4 holding rows rather than transactions.

A Form 4 Table I reports two kinds of row. A transaction row carries a trade and
the position left after it; a holding row carries a position with no trade at
all, which is how an insider discloses stock held through trusts, partnerships
and retirement plans. An analyst who reads only the transaction stream never
sees those positions, and the omission is not random: in this window holding
rows are overwhelmingly indirect while transaction rows are overwhelmingly
direct.

Three conventions this case fixes, each because the alternative is defensible
but wrong on this data:

1. ``shrs_ownd_folwng_trans`` on a transaction row is a running balance, not a
   delta. Within one filing 71.2% of transaction rows in this window share an
   ownership line with another row, so summing that column over transaction rows double counts.
   This case therefore never aggregates transaction balances; it counts rows.
2. A standing indirect position can be re-disclosed on later Form 4 filings. Summing
   holding rows across those filings can count it repeatedly: Walmart's Walton family
   trust line alone reports 3,002,673,393 shares on each of many filings and
   sums to 138.9 billion shares across 2024, against 8,033,386,215 shares
   outstanding on its 2024-12-04 cover page. Taking one filing per reporting owner is what makes a
   cross-sectional total meaningful.
3. A holding row and a transaction row inside the same filing can share
   ``(security_title, direct_indirect_ownership)`` while describing different
   vehicles, so the two row sets cannot be combined into a filing-level total
   without footnote text this runtime does not carry. The measured quantity is
   deliberately the holding-row side alone.

The window starts after NVIDIA's June 2024 ten-for-one split so that a single
issuer's share counts are on one basis; a window spanning the split would mix
pre- and post-split counts and make the outstanding-share ratio meaningless.
``security_title`` is not a grouping key: the selected issuer's own filings
carry both "Common Stock" and "Common".

The two indirect shares count rows, which the query states because weighting
them by the shares each row carries is equally defensible and gives a different
answer: 88.6274% of the holding-row shares and 6.7025% of the transaction-row
shares sit in indirect form, against the 83.6923% and 15.6661% of rows
reported. The row count is what the turn's argument needs, since the point is
how often each row type carries an indirect position rather than how much stock
does, and a row count is not dominated by a handful of very large trusts. The
contributing-owner count is not exposed the same way: none of the selected
issuer's eighteen retained holding rows carries zero shares, so counting owners
with any row and counting owners with a positive one both give six.

docstring:
Reconcile Form 4 derivative M rows with co-reported same-day sale prices.

SEC Form 4 code M means exercise or conversion of a derivative security exempt
under Rule 16b-3; it is not limited to employee stock options.  Code A means a
grant, award or other acquisition under Rule 16b-3(d).  A code and conversion
price do not supply grant-date fair value or identify all contractual economics.

The case uses an explicitly limited matching heuristic.  Each 2024 M row with a
positive reported conversion/exercise price and underlying-share count is joined
to the median nonderivative S price in the same accession and transaction date.
No transaction identifier links the derivative row to a particular sale, and
multiple M rows can share the same sale-price summary.  The resulting sale-price
minus conversion-price times underlying shares is therefore a signed co-reported
price-gap proxy.  It is not realized intrinsic value, sale proceeds, compensation
income, or proof that the converted shares were sold.

Expiration dates describe reported remaining term for a mixed derivative
population; they do not prove voluntary early exercise or identify forfeited time
value.  The final turn joins unique M transaction dates to Fama-French daily
market-excess returns and compares event-date and all-2024 medians.  This is
descriptive timing context only, not evidence that the market caused an M event
or that an issuer-specific security moved with the broad factor.

The `insider_option_exercise` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to pairing an
exercise with a sale on any date in the same filing rather than the same date, to
using the mean rather than the median co-reported sale price, to admitting
non-positive strikes, to ranking issuers by M row count rather than by the price-gap
proxy, to defining the event population as M rows rather than unique M dates, and to
admitting Form 5 alongside Form 4. The filing-type scope is the one worth naming: ten
2024 code-M rows arrive on Form 5, the annual late-report obligation, and admitting
them moves the M count from 8,503 to 8,513, the priced count from 4,158 to 4,168, the
count carrying an expiration date from 3,817 to 3,827, and the median reported price
from 41.4000 to 41.2500 USD. Inside the usable-term window the dated count moves from
3,806 to 3,807, which flips the median remaining term from 604.5000 to 604.0000 days
because the count changes parity. Form 5 is a
different filing obligation rather than a variant of Form 4, so the query names the

docstring:
Leverage is a definition before it is a number, and goodwill sits inside it.

A filer's balance sheet supports several defensible leverage ratios and the
gap between them is not small. Of the 5,524 annual filings in this window, 709
tag long-term debt, its noncurrent portion, the operating lease liability,
goodwill and stockholders' equity together, and 624 of those carry positive
equity. Across those 624 the median ratio to equity runs 0.6305 on the
noncurrent portion of long-term debt alone, 0.6805 on the whole of it, and
0.7852 once the operating lease liability joins the numerator. Struck in
aggregate against tangible equity instead, the lease-inclusive figure is
1.4399. The same balance sheets, read four defensible ways.

Each step is a real choice. The noncurrent portion excludes debt maturing
inside a year, so a filer refinancing next year looks less levered on it than
it is. The operating lease liability has sat on the balance sheet since the
2019 leases standard and is a contractual obligation the filer cannot walk
away from, but the conventional definition of debt leaves it out; here it adds
419.849886 USD billions against equity of 3394.290464. Goodwill is 1612.234198
of that equity, so removing it takes the denominator down by nearly half, and
138 of the 624 are left with negative tangible equity: their goodwill is
larger than their whole book.

Where that goodwill sits is a separate question, because impairment is tested
below the entity. 180 filers break goodwill out along a business-segment axis
inside the very filing that carries their entity figure, and for 162 the
segment figures sum to that total. The other 18 do not, and the query keeps
only the 162 rather than guessing which member to drop. Among the 162 the
largest segment carries a median 63.5991% of the goodwill and 125 of them have
a single segment holding more than half, so the entity-level ratio understates
how concentrated the impairment exposure is.

Four things the data forces:

1. ``LongTermDebt`` and ``LongTermDebtNoncurrent`` are different concepts and
   the file carries both. On 23 of the 709 the total is below the noncurrent
   portion, which the two tags cannot both be right about; they are reported
   rather than corrected, since nothing here says which one is wrong.
2. The ratios are struck only where equity is positive. A negative denominator
   turns a more levered filer into a smaller-looking ratio.
3. Every median is taken with linear interpolation. It matters: the 624 are an
   even count whose two middle values differ on all three ratios, so the lower
   and upper middle values give 0.6293 and 0.6317 against the reported 0.6305,
   0.6802 and 0.6809 against 0.6805, and 0.7837 and 0.7867 against 0.7852.
4. Segment rows are matched on the accession as well as the filer and period
   end. Matching on the period end alone would let a later annual report's
   comparative column stand against the earlier filing's entity total; inside
   one filing a member can still appear under more than one presentation
   index, and only index 0 is taken. Both rules bite: 133 of the 693 member
   groups in the window carry more than one row, 102 of them across filings
   and 31 inside one, and 17 carry more than one value. After the accession
   match 582 groups survive, 32 of them still holding more than one row but
   only one holding more than one value: Celanese reports EngineeredMaterials
   twice in the same filing, 5,025 USD millions at index 0 against 5,000 at
   index 1. Taking the highest index instead of index 0 drops the tie count
   to 161, the median share to 63.0318% and the majority count to 124, while
   leaving the matched filer count at 180. Every one of the 582 groups carries
   an index 0 row, so the rule selects rather than discards.

5. The segment median is also an even count whose middle values differ, at
   63.0318 and 64.1664 against the reported 63.5991, so the interpolation rule
   carries it too.

6. The aggregate after goodwill sums every filer in, including the 138 whose
   own equity after goodwill is below zero. Dropping them, which following the
   turn's own reading of a negative denominator would suggest, gives 0.9202
   rather than 1.4399. The aggregate stays well defined where the individual
   ratios do not, which is the reason for reporting it beside them.

Every stated selection binds except one: nine filers close twice inside the
window, seven of them at different period ends and two on different filing
dates, so the accession never has to separate them. The rule is stated anyway
and the case test asserts it does not fire.

One relation worth naming so it is not mistaken for an oversight: the
lease-inclusive aggregate on equity can be rebuilt from the debt aggregate
plus the lease total over the equity total, which is three reported figures
rather than two, and it lands on the same value either way. It is reported
because it is the comparison the turn is about.

docstring:
Compare a net-redemption proxy with gross money-fund flow activity.

The 2023 amendments to the money market fund rules require an institutional prime
or institutional tax exempt fund to impose a liquidity fee on a day when net
redemptions exceed 5 percent of net assets, unless the liquidity costs the fund
incurs are de minimis. The threshold is written on net flow, which is the
difference between what came in and what went out. Gross subscriptions plus
redemptions instead measure two-way transaction activity; they are not the
liquidity a portfolio had to raise.

The daily flow file reports 247,400 rows at the share class level across 1,053
classes, while net assets are reported once per series filing. A series files once
per period, and an amendment supersedes the filing it corrects, so the population
keeps the latest filing for each series period before the classes are summed:
2,419 series-days are covered by both an original N-MFP3 and its N-MFP3/A, and 226
of those pairs report different flows, so retaining both would enter the same day
twice with two different answers. Summing the classes of the retained filing on
each day gives 71,931 series-day observations over 316 series, a median of 2
classes each.

Dividing a daily flow by net assets needs care, because the asset figure is dated
the series report date at the end of the period while the flow is dated within it.
A fund that shrank sharply is measured against what was left. 492 series-days
report net assets below one million dollars, and 17 observations put a single day's
net flow beyond 100 percent of the fund's assets. Requiring at least a million
dollars leaves 71,439 observations, and even there the largest single-day net
redemption reaches -176.9093 percent of the reported base, so the ratio remains an
approximation rather than a measurement.

On that screened population the median absolute net balance is 0.3033 percent of
assets and median gross activity is 1.1841 percent. Their ratio has a median of
3.2406, computed on the 66,246 observations where net flow is not zero: 5,193 days,
7.2691 percent, show none, and 5,168 of those show no flow at all. Government funds
show a median 1.5743 percent gross-activity day against 0.8551 for prime.

Counted against 5 percent of the same period-end denominator, the two proxies do not
describe the same construct. Net redemptions exceed 5 percent on 1,788 series-days;
gross activity exceeds 5 percent on 15,783, a factor of 8.8272. Government funds
cross the gross line on 26.1362 percent of their days while prime funds cross the
net line on 0.8527 percent of theirs. Prime and the two tax-exempt categories,
which can contain covered funds, hold 18,895 of the screened days and 182 of the
1,788 proxy net crossings, 10.1790 percent. The file does not identify which series
are institutional.

The `money_fund_flow_trigger` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to retaining
share-class grain, dropping the analytic asset screen, using redemptions rather than
net flow, changing the percentage threshold, narrowing the category screen, and
retaining superseded filings instead of the latest one per series period. The query
fixes the reported convention, so these are robustness comparisons rather than
hidden answer paths.

Measurement boundary: flows are reported per share class while assets are reported
per series, and the available asset figure is a period-end snapshot rather than the
daily net asset base used by the rule.

Boundaries: the file carries no institutional or retail designation, so the
category screen is not a count or proven upper bound of funds subject to the rule,
and the fee is owed only when the estimated fee is not de minimis, which nothing
here observes. The threshold in the rule is evaluated by the fund on its own daily
asset base, which this file does not carry, so the ratios here are built on a period
end figure instead. The mandatory-fee compliance date was 2024-10-02 while the flow
file opens on 2024-06-03; the 1,136 series-days that precede it are 1.5902 percent
of the screened population and carry 3 of the 1,788 net crossings and none of the
182 in the fee-eligible categories, so the overlap does not move any figure
reported here.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for
N requested decimals; counts and fund names match exactly.
