docstring:
Measure share-class gross-to-net yield wedges within money market series.

A money market fund reports a seven-day gross yield at the series level and a
seven-day net yield for each share class. The runtime class-yield table pairs the
series-level gross figure with each class-level net figure. At the 2025-06-30
yield date the file carries
1,062 class rows across 308 series; 183 series report more than one class, and in
all 183 the gross yield is identical across every class the series reports. The
case defines the difference between the paired gross and net fields as a wedge;
it does not treat that constructed wedge as a stated expense ratio.

The wedge is not small and is not evenly borne. On the 1,008 class rows that
survive the stated anomaly screen, the median class gives up 33.0000 basis
points and the mean 39.5427. Weighting instead by the assets in each class, a
dollar gives up 21.4018 basis points. The gap between 39.5427 and 21.4018 is the
whole point: higher-asset classes carry lower wedges in this observed population,
so the average class and the average dollar are not answering the same question.
The source does not by itself establish an investor-type or causal explanation.
The widest class pays 234.0000 basis points,
and within Allspring Money Market Fund alone the cheapest and dearest classes sit
116.0000 basis points apart on an identical portfolio.

The screen matters because the field is not always populated. At the same date 29
rows report a net yield of exactly zero against a positive gross yield, and 15 of
those belong to a class holding no assets at all; across the file 274 rows report a
net yield above the gross yield. That ordering is inconsistent with treating the
paired fields as gross-before-expenses and net-after-expenses, so the case screens
the rows as anomalies. The screen does not establish whether the source filing,
field matching, rounding or another data issue caused any individual observation.

Coverage is the other thing that has to be checked before any change over time is
computed. Of the 11,931 yield rows dated before 2025, 11,909, or 99.8156 percent,
come from amended filings; the original filings begin only at the end of 2024. In
June 2024 just 79 share classes appear against 1,029 in June 2025, so the early
window is a sample of funds that later amended rather than a picture of the
industry, and an unqualified industry-wide difference against the later window is
not supported. A comparison restricted to an explicitly common observed sample
would answer a different question. Within the available 2025 table, the
asset-weighted gross yield falls from 4.4327 percent in
January to 4.0241 in November while the three-month Treasury bill averages fall
from 4.3429 to 3.9372: declines of 40.86 and 40.57 basis points, with fund yields
sitting a little above bills at both ends.

Measured rejected alternatives, from the `money_market_fee_wedge` comparison, include retaining anomalous rows, substituting the equal-class mean for the
asset-weighted result, using the net yield alone instead of the defined difference,
and treating the observed June 2024 and June 2025 populations as comparable
industry snapshots. The query explicitly requests the relevant screen, both
weighting views and the coverage diagnostic, so these are instruction-following
probes rather than a live hidden-method trap. This is a hard baseline case.

Knowledge the case assumes and does not supply: that Form N-MFP reports the gross
yield at the series level and the net yield at the class level, that an average
over classes and an average over dollars answer different questions, and that an
amended filing is not an independent fund observation.

Boundaries: a seven-day yield is an annualized snapshot rather than a realized
return, and the wedge inferred from it is a yield reduction rather than a stated

docstring:
Reconcile NFIP payment components against the coverage each one actually consumes.

A flood policy is not one pot of money.  The building coverage, the contents
coverage and increased cost of compliance are three statutory coverages with
three separate limits, and a payment made under one of them does not draw down
another.  Increased cost of compliance in particular is additional coverage: it
carries its own USD30,000 cap and sits outside the building limit entirely.

The trap is the second turn, which asks how many claims exhausted their building
coverage.  Only the gross building payment is drawn against the building
coverage.  Summing the payment components before the comparison reports 12,097
claims when increased cost of compliance is folded in, 18,137 when the contents
payment is folded in and 18,308 when both are, against 11,934 on the pinned
reading; the same fold-in carries the exhausted group's gross building payment
to USD2,262.423430 million against USD2,233.450134 million.  Counts are compared
for exact equality and the payment is pinned to six decimals, so the
rounding-boundary tolerance of 0.6e-6 excludes every one of those readings --
the smallest of them misses by 163 claims and by USD28.973296 million.  The
error propagates into the third turn, where the count of exhausted claims that
also drew increased cost of compliance (229, carrying USD4.936133 million) is
the evidence that the coverage pays past an exhausted building limit.

The first turn carries a second, independent axis.  The cause-of-damage column
stores the same code in two representations: 133,349 rows read "4" and a further
12,564 read "4.0".  Reading the column as recorded reports 19 distinct causes and
a leading cause of 133,349 claims; coercing it to a number instead silences the
702 rows carrying the letter codes A, B, C and D and reports 8 distinct causes.
The pinned reading treats a code as one cause regardless of numeric formatting
and keeps the letter codes, giving 12 causes and 145,913 claims.  Both counts are
compared for exact equality, so both naive readings are excluded.  The pinned
answer does not depend on how the formatting is reconciled: casting to an integer,
stripping a trailing ".0" as text, and casefolding before either all give 12 and
145,913.  Numeric coercion recovers the leading count but not the cause count, so
the two outputs fail the two naive readings between them.

Rejected conventions.  Building coverage counts as exhausted when the gross
building payment reaches it, not only when it passes it -- 11,140 of the 11,934
settle at exactly the coverage amount and passing alone would report 794.  Storm
rows are restricted to the ones carrying a recorded flood cause; on the frozen
extract those are exactly the 49,617 rows labelled Flash Flood, Flood or Debris
Flow, and every one of them already sits on a county, so the county-granularity
filter below is a guard that currently removes nothing.  It is what the restriction
costs that matters: 5,485 water-related rows -- Tropical Storm, Coastal Flood, Storm
Surge/Tide, Hurricane, Lakeshore Flood, Tsunami -- carry no cause at all and are filed
against a forecast zone, so coastal and tropical flooding never enters the pairing.
The storm side is restricted to the fifty states and the District of Columbia,
which settles a reading rather than changing an answer: the territories are
numbered outside the standard range and could never have paired as recorded, so
the restriction moves none of the sixteen figures, while a reader who repaired
the numbering instead would report 6,877 shared county-months, 138,693 matched
claims, USD13,816.571187 million unmatched and 6,284 on the leading cause.  The
month is the month of loss on the claim side and the month the event began on
the storm side.  683 claim rows carry no county code at all; they can never be
paired and the query counts them outside the pairing, which is worth
USD21.153562 million of the unmatched total -- dropping them instead would report
USD13,797.319565 million, so the rule is stated rather than left to the reader.

Sixteen combinations of payment basis, comparison boundary and coverage scope were
swept over the second turn and exactly one reproduces the pinned pair.  The three
dollar outputs lie 0.31, 0.18 and 0.11 of a unit from the value they are rounded
to -- a rounding boundary would be half a unit away -- and are invariant to
summation order to the cent.

Link the largest 2020 OFR FSI jump to same-day industry dispersion.

Across 253 dates common to OFR and the Ken French 10-industry portfolios, the
largest single-step FSI increase between consecutive common dates is 3.454 points from 1.680 on 2020-03-06
to 5.134 on 2020-03-09.  Volatility is the largest category-contribution
increase at 2.178 points.  On the event date all ten industry portfolios are
negative: Enrgy is worst at -19.68%, Shops is best at -5.05%, their equal-
weighted mean is -8.531%, and the cross-industry spread is 14.63 points.

largest rise over a run of consecutive dates of any length rather than a single
step, shifting industry returns to the next common date, ranking category levels
rather than changes, or using the median industry return changes at least one
output.  The
query pins these conventions, so they are regression probes for a hard baseline.

OFR-only event grid is a measured numerical equivalent in this frozen sample.

var_desc: Store the count of reconciling filers tagging a discount rate as an integer.
query: Keep the filers that reconcile exactly and tag the weighted-average operating lease discount rate, stored as a fraction, at the same 2024 balance date. Compare each with the five-year Treasury par yield on that date, or the latest earlier date with a yield. Report how many filers that is, their median rate, how many rates stand strictly below the yield, and the median of rate less yield. Explain what rate a lessee discounts its lease payments with, and what to make of a reported rate below the Treasury yield.
docstring:
An operating lease liability is a present value at rates fixed in the past.

Under the 2016 lease standard a lessee discounts each operating lease's
remaining payments at the rate implicit in the lease or, usually, its
incremental borrowing rate, both set when the lease begins. Existing leases
are not remeasured when market rates move, so the weighted-average discount
rate a filer reports is an average of rates fixed over many years.

Among the large filers' 2024 annual reports, 372 tag the undiscounted lease
payments, the amount representing interest and the operating lease liability
at the same date, and 359 reconcile exactly: payments less interest equal the
liability. One filer tags its interest as a negative amount. The median
interest is 17.0856 percent of undiscounted payments.

Of the 339 filers that reconcile and tag a discount rate, 166 report a
weighted rate below the five-year Treasury par yield on their balance date;
in 2021 only one of them did. Between 2021 and 2024 the filers' rates rose a
median 100 basis points while the five-year yield on their balance dates rose
312. A rate below the Treasury yield cannot be what the company would pay to
borrow today; it is what it paid when its leases began. 2022 is the first year
in which more than half of these filers stood below the yield.

The right-of-use asset starts from the liability and is adjusted for prepaid
and accrued rent, lease incentives, initial direct costs and impairment. 281
of the 328 filers tagging it carry an asset below the liability, at a median
0.9348 of it.

Readings measured so they are not mistaken for oversights:

1. Every value is taken as first reported: from the earliest-filed annual
   report carrying it at that date. 48 discount-rate values differ between the
   first and the latest report carrying them. Reading the latest report gives
   358 exact reconciliations, 338 rate filers at a median 4.31 percent, 165
   below the yield, 329 paired filers, and 280 of 327 assets below the
   liability.
2. Each figure keeps the sign it is tagged with. Reading the negative interest
   amount as its absolute value lets that filer reconcile, giving 360 rather
   than 359 exact reconciliations.
3. The balance date in a calendar year is the latest date in that year at
   which an annual report tags the item. In 2019, 45 filers tag the liability
   at two dates; for 42 of them the earlier is 2019-01-01, the opening balance
   on adopting the standard, and the later is the fiscal year end.
4. The comparison yield is the five-year par yield published on the balance
   date or, where none was published that day, the latest earlier date. On
   the ten-year point 2024 has 199 rather than 166 filers below.
5. Two rates are tagged on the wrong scale: 32000 for one filer at 2019 and
   3.1 for another at 2021, both as first reported. Leaving them out or
   dividing them by 100 moves no output. One 2022 rate equals the yield on its
   balance date; reading "below" as "at or below" would not change the first
   majority year.
6. The median interest share is taken across all 372 filers tagging the
   schedule; across only the 359 that reconcile it is 17.0735. Reading each
   item at the latest 2024 date where all three are tagged together, or the
   rate and asset at their own latest 2024 dates, gives the same populations.

Report the median change in that yield between the two year ends, how many rate changes lie within 50 basis points of it, inclusive, and, at the 2022 year end, the median rate, how many rates stand strictly below the yield, and the median of rate less yield. docstring:
A pension obligation is remeasured at current rates every year.

A sponsor discounts its pension benefits at a rate read at each measurement
date from yields on high-quality corporate bonds whose timing matches the
benefit payments. Unlike a lease rate, which is fixed when the lease begins,
the pension rate is reset every year, so it moves with market yields and the
obligation moves with it.

Among the large filers' annual reports, 124 tag a discount rate for their
defined benefit pension plans at both their 2021 and 2022 year ends. One of
them tags a negative 2022 rate, which cannot be a discount rate. For the other
123 the rate rose a median 250 basis points while the ten-year Treasury par
yield on the same dates rose a median 236, and 118 rate changes lie within 50
basis points of the yield change. At the 2022 year end the median rate is 5.20
percent, a median 132 basis points above the ten-year yield, and only 4 stand
below it: high-quality corporate bonds carry a credit spread over Treasuries.

Rising rates shrink the obligation's present value, which the sponsor records
as an actuarial gain. 112 of the filers carry the 2022 gain and the obligation
at both year ends. 20 tag the gain below zero, and every one of those shows a
lower obligation at the end of the year: a sign convention, not a loss. The
gain's size over the opening obligation, per unit of rate change, implies a
median duration of 9.0457 years. All 108 filers that carry plan assets with
the year's return lost money on those assets, yet 71 of them ended the year
with assets less obligation strictly higher, and the median funded ratio rose from 0.9495
to 0.9794.

Readings measured so they are not mistaken for oversights:

1. Only the primary presentation (presentation index 0) is read. Narrative
   restatements at other indexes round the same fact, as 3,668 against 3,700
   million for one filer's 2022 gain; reading them gives values the tables do
   not carry.
2. Every value is taken as first reported, from the earliest-filed annual
   report carrying it. Reading the latest report instead gives 2 invalid
   rates, 117 tracking, 111 gain filers with 21 negative, a median duration of
   9.0623, and 70 of 106 losing plans improving out of 107.
3. Filers whose rate is not strictly between zero and one at either date are
   left out. Reading the negative rate as its absolute value admits that filer
   and gives 119 tracking, 113 gain filers, 21 negative, 9.0623 years, and 72
   of 109 improving.
4. The comparison yield is the ten-year par yield on the year-end date or the
   latest earlier date. On the twenty-year point 103 rates track and the
   median spread is 106; on the thirty-year point 71 track and it is 123.
5. The implied duration divides the gain's size by the opening obligation and
   by the rate change as a decimal. The signed gain gives 8.7768, the closing
   obligation 12.4858 and the average obligation 10.5787.
6. "Strictly higher" matters: one losing plan ends with an unchanged funded
   position, so "at least as high" gives 72.

    # recompute derivative for new curve
    def wk_deriv(t, tj, u_inf, alpha):
        W = wilson_kernel(t, tj, u_inf, alpha)
        if t < tj:

var_desc: Store its trades' settlement date as an ISO YYYY-MM-DD string.
query: Repeat the first turn for January through April 2024: report the busiest trading day, the settlement date of its trades, and the shares failed on that settlement date. Explain how you matched the dates.
docstring:
Lining up fails-to-deliver with the trades that produced them.

The SEC fails-to-deliver files are dated by settlement date, while FINRA's
daily short-volume file is dated by trading day. A trade settles a fixed number
of settlement days later: two before 2024-05-28 and one from that trading day
on. Settlement days are the days the depository settles: weekdays other than
Federal Reserve holidays and Good Friday. A bank holiday on which the stock
market trades (Columbus Day, Veterans Day) is therefore not a settlement day,
while a day the market closed and the depository did not (2025-01-09, the
national day of mourning) still is.

Trap. Reading the trade-to-settlement step with the wrong cycle is the
plausible wrong path, and it first becomes live in turn 1. The 2025 trading day
with the largest reported volume is 2025-04-09; its trades settled on
2025-04-10, when 515,030,616 shares stood failed across all securities. A
two-day cycle reads 2025-04-11 and 398,091,073; matching the trading day
itself reads 268,107,061. In turn 2 the largest rise into the settlement date
is DMN's 98,318,799 shares; on the two-day reading DMN still leads but with
97,607,770. In turn 3 the wrong path runs the other way: the busiest day in
January through April 2024 is 2024-01-16, whose trades settled on 2024-01-18
under the two-day cycle then in force, with 118,542,824 shares failed, while a
one-day reading gives 2024-01-17 and 121,872,221. In turn 4 a one-day reading
puts the 2024-05-24 trades on 2024-05-28 rather than 2024-05-29, and a
trading-day calendar puts the 2025-01-08 trades on 2025-01-10 and the
2025-10-10 trades on 2025-10-13, a day with no settlement record. Each wrong
date fails exact matching, and each wrong share count differs by far more than
the rounding-boundary tolerance, which is zero for integer counts.

The cycle is visible in the data. Around symbol-days whose reported volume
exceeds ten times the median of the previous twenty trading days and one
million shares, the average fails balance rises most two trading days later
for spikes from 2024-01-03 through 2024-05-20 (by 196,968 shares, over 3,474
events) and one trading day later for spikes from 2024-06-03 on (by 271,282
shares, over 17,269 events).

Readings measured so they are not mistaken for oversights:

1. Volume is the short-volume file's total volume for the day, summed over
   symbols. The busiest 2025 day leads the next, 2025-10-22, by 458,653,085
   shares; the busiest early-2024 day leads 2024-03-04 by 174,121,428. Ranking
   by short volume instead picks 2025-06-12 for 2025 (and the same 2024-01-16
   for early 2024), so the query names total volume.
2. Balances are summed over every row on the date. Four symbol-dates carry two
   rows (different CUSIPs under one symbol); the rise in turn 2 sums them per
   symbol and reads a symbol absent on a date as zero. The runner-up, SUNE,
   rose 96,204,262.
3. The settlement calendar is taken as weekdays less Federal Reserve holidays
   and Good Friday, and reproduces the file's 499 settlement dates exactly.
   Federal Reserve holidays alone would add 2024-03-29 and 2025-04-18, two Good
   Fridays the file does not settle on; no output falls near either.

docstring:
Measure payout composition across alternative SEC cash-flow concepts.

The case builds one profitable-filer population from full-year 2024 Company
Facts windows, then compares a common-stock-only dividend measure with a total
dividend measure. `PaymentsOfDividends` includes distributions to common and
preferred shareholders and noncontrolling interests, so the total-dividend rule
uses that concept when present and falls back to
`PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock` only when the broader concept is absent. This is
a dataset reading convention, not an assertion that the concepts are identical.

The later turns carry that measure into company-level payout composition and
identify the largest repurchaser and dividend payer. SEC MIDAS daily stock
volume supplies independent market-liquidity context for those two issuers; it
does not explain their payout policy or establish a causal relation between
trading activity and distributions.

Measured rejected alternatives cover the common-stock-only
measure, loss-making filers, first-filed duplicates, unrestricted reporting
windows and a mismatched market-data window. The query pins each convention, so
this is a hard baseline rather than a hidden-method trap.

Boundaries: absence of one concept is not evidence that no dividend was paid;
fiscal years ending in different 2024 months cover different twelve-month
periods; a payout above annual net income is not an arithmetic inconsistency;
and cross-sectional medians do not describe every firm's channel choice.
Numeric validation uses the shared rounding tolerance; counts and identifiers
match exactly.

docstring:
A SOFR average is compounded on business days, with simple interest across gaps.

The New York Fed publishes 30-, 90- and 180-day SOFR averages each business
day. Each covers the calendar days from the date that many days before the
publication date up to the day before it. A daily rate earns simple interest
for every calendar day until the next business day, so a Friday rate covers
the weekend in one simple step; interest compounds only from one business day
to the next; and the year has 360 days. Where the window opens on a day that is
not a business day, the rate of the preceding business day covers it until the
next one. Rounded half up to five decimals, that calculation reproduces all 748
publication dates from 2023 through 2025 on all three windows, and the SOFR
Index itself steps the same way from one business day to the next.

Every competing reading reproduces none of the 748 on any window. Compounding
every calendar day differs from the reproducing value by a median 0.000313,
0.000333 and 0.000337 percentage points on the three windows; a 365-day year
by 0.000125, 0.000397 and 0.000804; a simple average weighting each calendar
day equally by 0.009102, 0.028897 and 0.058227. Five decimals separate all of
them. Shifting the window a day later or earlier under the reproducing
calculation matches 115 or 111 of the 748 30-day averages. The case reports the
unrounded 2025-12-31 values, 3.7865938 on the 30-day window and 4.1999627 on
the 180-day window, which each competing reading moves.

The gap between the compounded and the simple day-weighted average is interest
on interest. Over 2023 to 2025 it has a median of 0.9102 basis points on the
30-day window and 5.8227 on the 180-day window, and reaches 7.0790, growing
with the window and with the level of rates.

The curve quotes the one-month bill on a 365-day bond-equivalent basis. The
first cut in the target range the table carries falls on 2024-09-19. Before
it, the published 30-day average reads a median 18.626 basis points below the
curve's 1-month point, and 11.232 below once restated to a 365-day year; from
that date on it reads 0.262 above, and 6.313 above once restated. The basis is
worth roughly five days' interest. The change of sign is the difference between
a rate already fixed over the past month and a yield that prices the month
ahead.

The averages lag the policy rate by their window. The 30-day window first
holds only rates fixed on or after the 2024-09-19 cut on 2024-10-21, and the
180-day window on 2025-03-18; on 2024-10-21 the published 30-day average
stands 45.488 basis points below the published 180-day average, which still
holds pre-cut rates. Reading the window start as the calendar day itself,
without carrying a non-business day back to the preceding fixing, gives the
same two dates here.

Nearest cases, recorded for the portfolio checkpoint. The retired
single-source sofr_index_financing_cost took one year's financing cost from
the index ratio and set it against an arithmetic mean of fixings, close to
this case's second turn. What is new here is recovering the averaging
convention from the published averages themselves, which the index does not
settle on its own, and the fourth turn's pass-through lag. The active
treasury_bill_discount_investment_rate_basis converts bill quotes between
bases; here the basis step is one comparison inside a question about
in-arrears averages.

Three conventions the query states because each moves an output:

1. Medians use linear interpolation. The 748 publication dates are an even
   count whose middle values differ on both premium series; the 429 and 319
   dates either side of the first cut are odd, so there the rule is stated and
   does not bind.
2. The first cut is read from the target range the table itself carries, as
   the first date whose upper bound is below the previous reported date's.
3. The premium is taken on the unrounded reproducing average, not the
   published five-decimal figure. The published figure reads 0.9103, 5.8223
   and 7.0787 against the reported 0.9102, 5.8227 and 7.0790.

import numpy as np

# Final verification of the risk-neutral calibration
k = 0.22262324603897557
sigma = 0.9585289029756857
r0 = 4.49
theta_star = -2.2737220137622787
coupon_annual = 4.38
principal = 100
n_payments = 10
coupon_half = coupon_annual/2

def vasicek_zcb(tau, theta, r0, k, sigma):
    B = (1 - np.exp(-k*tau))/k
    A = (B - tau)*(theta - sigma**2/(2*k**2)) - sigma**2 * B**2/(4*k)
    return np.exp(-B*r0 + A)

def bond_price(theta):
    price = 0.0
    for i in range(1, n_payments+1):
        tau = i*0.5
        price += coupon_half * vasicek_zcb(tau, theta, r0, k, sigma)
    price += principal * vasicek_zcb(5.0, theta, r0, k, sigma)
    return price

docstring:
Separate the Form 13F cover-page scale change from the filer-level holding unit.

Two unit conventions sit in the same 13F data and are routinely conflated. The
cover-page value total moved to whole dollars for filings made from 2023-01-03:
across original holdings reports the median raw cover total per holding row rises from
4,045.1296 at 2022-09-30 to 2,566,876.9847 at 2022-12-31, a factor of 634.5599, so
summing the field across that boundary produces a 155.5334-fold step that is a units
artifact. The holding rows carry a separate, per-filer unit that the governed
tables infer: at 2022-12-31, 5,758 filings report holdings in dollars and 1,308
in thousands, while the cover page reads as dollar scale for 5,799 and thousands
scale for 1,267. The two classifications agree on 96.5610 percent of filings but
disagree on 243, so one cannot be used as per-filing metadata for the other.

Reading the already-normalized holdings aggregation instead gives 75.484185
trillion USD over 36,120 issuer rows at 2022-12-31, led by Apple Inc. at
1.464846 trillion USD across 4,569 filing accessions. Dividing that USD total by
the raw, mixed-scale cover-page sum produces the number 2.1700, but not a
unit-consistent ratio. Carrying that issuer into the
registrant universe, its 10,535,889,677 reported shares stand against
15,821,946,000 shares outstanding as of 2023-01-20 from the latest count filed on
or before 2023-02-15, a 66.5904 percent reported-shares quotient. It is not total
institutional or beneficial ownership: the reporting population, security scope,
measurement dates, and shared-discretion reporting all differ. 974 of the 7,066
filings include other managers' holdings, but that count does not quantify duplicate
shares.

The `thirteen_f_unit_break` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to including
amendments, rescaling the cover page with the holding-row convention, changing the
cover heuristic, ranking by shares, and selecting a different outstanding-share
fact. The query fixes the reported convention, so these are robustness comparisons
rather than hidden answer paths.

The counts are of filings, not of filers. Three managers submit a duplicate qualifying
report with identical totals -- CIK 1767435 at 2022-09-30, CIK 93751 and CIK 1016021 at
2022-12-31 -- so collapsing to distinct filers reports 6,744 and 7,064 instead of 6,745
and 7,066. The medians and sums are taken over the same per-filing population.

Two source fields have to agree before a filing counts as an original holdings
report. One restatement per period carries submission type 13F-HR while its own
amendment flag reads Y, so filtering on the submission type alone admits it and
reports 6,746 and 7,067. Excluding it is what the query's "every amendment" asks
for, and it moves the two medians, both ratios, four of the six classification
counts and the other-managers count.

Two boundaries are load bearing. The cover-page scale is a per-filing property,
not a rule that holds without exception: 8.54 percent of filings for periods
from 2022Q4 still read as thousands scale and 9.29 percent of earlier filings
read as dollar scale, so the query classifies each filing rather than assuming
the period. The 100,000 reported-units-per-row cut is stated in the query because
nothing in the data labels each cover-page value's scale. It is an analytic
heuristic, not a consequence of the statutory $100 million manager threshold.
Sweeping it from 20,000 to 500,000 puts the disagreement count at
374, 263, 243, 250 and 416, so 100,000 sits at the minimum, the point where the
cover-page reading agrees most closely with the independently inferred
holding-row unit. The answer is fixed by the query either way.

Fragility: the leading issuer is 2.4829 percent ahead of the runner-up in
reported value, 1.464846 against 1.428476 trillion USD, so the top of the
ranking is a two-name race rather than a wide margin; the frozen artifact fixes
it.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for
N requested decimals; counts, identifiers and names match exactly.

query: The monthly statement of the public debt lists every marketable Treasury security outstanding at each month end, and for the inflation-protected ones it reports separately how much of the principal has accrued with the price index. Working from the security-level rows and leaving the file's published class totals aside, report how many month ends the file covers and, at the last of them, how many inflation-protected rows it carries, how many distinct securities those rows describe, and the outstanding balance summed across those rows in billions of dollars. Explain why the row count and the security count differ.
docstring:
Reconcile the accrued inflation compensation on TIPS against the daily flow.

An inflation-protected Treasury owes more principal than the Treasury borrowed.
The principal accretes with the price index, and the accrued amount is debt that
was never issued.  At 2025-12-31 it is USD385.656277 billion against
USD2,133.881769 billion of TIPS outstanding -- 18.072992 percent of the principal
the Treasury owes on them.

Two publications record it differently.  The monthly statement carries the
accrued amount as a **stock** beside each security, and its aggregate closes
exactly: issued plus accrued plus redeemed equals outstanding on every one of the
84 month ends, the largest residual across all of them being 5e-10 of a million
dollars.  The daily statement carries the accretion as a **flow**, one
transaction line per business day, 1,757 of them, 323 of which are negative
because the index fell.

The two do not meet, and the reason is the distinction the case turns on.  When a
security matures, the accrued principal it carried leaves the stock; the flow
never gives it back.  Over the 83 months both files cover, 22 month ends lose a
security and USD204.679361 billion of accrued principal leaves with them.
Comparing the month-to-month change in the stock with the sum of that month's
daily flow leaves a mean absolute gap of USD2,512.193653 million and reverses the
sign in 7 months.  Taking out the accrued principal that left brings the mean
absolute gap to USD48.235140 million, a fifty-two-fold reduction, with the worst
month at USD271.452971 million.  July 2025 is the clearest case: the stock fell
by USD10,197.547 million while the flow added USD4,387 million, because one
security matured carrying USD14,438.975 million of accrued principal.

Rejected conventions.  The stock is read from the security-level detail rows, not
the published class totals, which appear in the same file and would double count.
A security-level outstanding balance is reported once per security while issued
and accrued amounts are reported on each issue row, so the aggregate closes even
though only 53 of the final month end's 134 rows carry an outstanding balance.
Redemptions are stored as negative numbers and enter the identity as they stand.
The residual gap that survives the maturity adjustment is a settlement-timing
difference between a daily transaction file and a month-end snapshot, and the
case reports it rather than forcing it to zero.

query: Return to the auction records. Report the index level for September 2025 and the 12-month inflation rate to September 2025 on the same basis as the first turn. Explain how you reached each month's level.
docstring:
Reading consumer-price inflation out of TIPS reference CPIs.

Treasury indexes inflation-protected securities to the CPI-U, not seasonally
adjusted, with a lag. The reference CPI for the first day of a month is the
index for the third preceding month; for later days it moves linearly toward
the index for the second preceding month, by the share of the month elapsed.
The auction records publish the reference CPI on each security's dated date
and issue date, so two reference values in one month solve for two monthly
indexes, and one value ties two neighbouring months together.

Trap. The auction records list reference CPIs on dates in every month, and the
plausible wrong path reads a reference value dated in July 2025 as the July
2025 index. That path first becomes live in turn 1. On 2025-07-15 the
reference CPI is 321.09758 and on 2025-07-31 it is 321.44339, against a July
index of 323.048; the 12-month rate it gives is 2.33 percent from the 15th or
2.35 from the 31st, against 2.70. The real-time data set offers a second
shortcut: its July 2025 figure, 2.38 percent first released and 2.77 most
recent, is a seasonally adjusted one-month change at an annual rate, and
compounding its twelve monthly changes gives 2.74, still not the unadjusted
12-month rate. At two decimals every one of these lies outside the
rounding-boundary tolerance of 0.006 around 2.70, and the reference values lie
at least 1.60 away from the level, far outside its 0.0006. July 2025 is chosen
because its index was published after most models' training data, so the
level has to be read from the records rather than recalled.

The correct path reads July 2025 and August 2025 from the two October 2025
reference values, and July 2024 the same way from October 2024. September 2025
follows from the single reference value on 2025-11-28 once August 2025 is
known. September 2024 follows from the value on 2024-12-31 once October 2024
is known from the January 2025 pair, and agrees to three decimals with the
route through 2024-11-29 and the August 2024 index (315.30133 against
315.30100).

The Bureau of Labor Statistics published no index for October 2025. The value
the December 2025 reference CPI implies, 325.604, is the September 2025 index
grown for one month at its 12-month rate: 324.800 times the twelfth root of
324.800 over 315.301 gives 325.6044, the substitute Treasury's rules prescribe
when a month's index is missing.

Readings measured so they are not mistaken for oversights:

1. Dated-date references are read from original issues only. A reopening row
   repeats the original security's dated-date reference, and in one row
   (the August 2025 reopening of the 30-year security) the date beside it reads
   2025-08-15 while the value is the 2025-02-15 reference; no output uses
   August 2025 dates, but reading that row as an August reference would solve
   May and June 2025 as 315.054 and 323.935.
2. Index levels are rounded to three decimals, as published, and the 12-month
   rates are taken from the rounded levels. From the unrounded solutions they
   are 2.7049 and 3.0126 percent, the same at two decimals.
3. The seasonally adjusted rates compound each annualized change to a monthly
   factor by its twelfth root. Averaging the annualized changes instead gives
   2.7502 from the most recent values.

var_desc: Store how many auctions take a 366-day year under the reproducing rule, as an integer.
query: From Treasury bill auctions issued 2023-01-01 through 2025-12-31, excluding cash management bills, report count. For bills with issue-to-maturity terms of at most 182 days, infer the calendar-year day count that reproduces each published high investment rate to three decimals from a simple return on its published high price per USD 100; report cohort count. Apply the inferred convention to all selected bills and report how many use 366 days. Explain the day-count rule and the distinction between published high discount and investment rates.
docstring:
A Treasury bill auction publishes two rates that measure different things.

The high discount rate states the discount from face value as an annual rate
on a 360-day year; the price per 100 follows from it exactly, and for every
one of the 867 regular bill auctions issued from 2023 through 2025 the
published price is 100 times one less the rate times the days to maturity
over 360, to the six decimals published. The high investment rate states the
return on the price paid, annualised over the bill's own year. Because the
price is below face and the year is longer than 360 days, the investment rate
is the higher of the two, by a median of 8.40 basis points on 4-week bills,
13.45 on 13-week, 18.65 on 26-week and 22.20 on 52-week bills.

The bill's own year is not decided by whether a 29 February falls inside the
bill's life. For the 821 auctions of bills running 182 days or fewer, the
published investment rate equals (100 - price) / price times y over the days
to maturity to three decimals for every auction only when y is the number of
days in the year that follows the issue date. A bill issued on 2023-03-07 and
maturing on 2023-04-04 takes y = 366 although its life contains no leap day,
and a bill issued on 2024-02-29 takes y = 365. Under that rule 273 of the 867
auctions carry a 366-day year. The competing rules reproduce fewer: a leap day
inside the bill's life 630 of 821 (and 81 at 366 days), the issue year being a
leap year 387, the maturity year being a leap year 522, a flat 365 days 563
and a flat 360 days none. The published price has to be used as published:
the price recomputed from the discount rate without its six-decimal rounding
reproduces 820 of the 821.

The difference splits into a day-count part, the discount rate times the
excess of y over 360 days, and a price part, the remainder from stating the
return on price rather than on face. The first depends on the rate level
alone, a median of 6.7167 basis points on 4-week bills and 6.6424 on 26-week;
the second grows with term, 1.6806 against 11.6583.

The par yield curve quotes bills on a coupon-equivalent basis. Set against the
curve on the auction date, the 26-week discount rate sits a median 18.50 basis
points below the 6-month point while the investment rate sits 0.00 from it;
the 52-week discount rate sits 23.00 below the 1-year point and the investment
rate 0.30 below. Every 26- and 52-week auction in the window has its
investment rate closer to the curve than its discount rate.

Three further conventions the query states because each moves an output:

1. Auctions are grouped by the term offered at that auction, as stated in
   weeks. 554 of the 867 are reopenings whose original term differs; grouped
   by original term the 26-week median difference reads 14.50 rather than
   18.65. The same offering also runs to a few different day counts, 143 of
   the 156 26-week auctions at 182 days and the rest at 181 or 183, so
   grouping by the day count instead gives 13.70, 18.90 and 22.45 for the
   13-, 26- and 52-week medians rather than 13.45, 18.65 and 22.20; only the
   4-week median is unchanged.
2. Cash management bills are left out. They run to irregular terms and would
   enter no offered-term group cleanly.
3. Medians are taken with linear interpolation. The 13-week and 26-week groups
   hold 156 auctions each, an even count whose two middle values differ.

Treasury bill discount earnings versus floating repo carry.

The fixed redemption discount on an auctioned bill and a daily SOFR-funded
purchase have different day-count bases and economic cash-flow timing. The
retrospective financing path is hypothetical, not a 2025 executable repo quote.
The published 4.15% high bank-discount rate is not an investor's cash-on-cash
annualized yield; the latter is 4.2978% under the stipulated ACT/365 convention.
Using a same-effective-day SOFR before publication gives USD200,148.286765
of baseline interest rather than USD200,184.999994; ACT/365 in place of repo
ACT/360 gives USD197,442.7397201. The model uses the
9 a.m. published-fixing reset specified in the query and a bill maturity date
excluded from financing accrual. The base 90%-advance loan has positive cash
carry of USD9,620.6000 before other risks and costs; a Sep 1 rate shock of
100 basis points makes it negative USD13,386.3568. These are baseline
convention probes, not a live diagnostic trap.

docstring:
Dynamic Nelson--Siegel forecast at the deepest SOFR-era inversion.

The case selects the common Treasury/SOFR date with the most negative 10-year
minus 2-year CMT spread, bootstraps every trailing curve into continuously
compounded zero yields, and estimates one shared Diebold--Li decay parameter by
panel least squares.  The parameter is identified by the global minimum on the
declared compact interval; date-specific level, slope and curvature factors are
linear conditional on that decay.

The terminal comparison estimates a full VAR(1) for the carried factor history
and forecasts the next Treasury curve date.  It compares the resulting curve
forecast with a factor random walk.  This is a retrospective analytical
benchmark, not a no-arbitrage production curve or evidence that inversion alone
predicts returns.  Repricing, conditional OLS orthogonality and VAR stability are
the numerical invariants.  Intermediate calculations retain full precision.

The `treasury_dns_forecast` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to treating reported
par yields as zero yields instead of bootstrapping them, to a 250-curve rather than
252-curve training window, and to estimating separate AR(1) factor dynamics rather than
a full VAR(1). The curve basis is the one worth naming: reading par as spot
skips the bootstrap entirely, so it changes every zero yield the factors are fitted to
rather than only the forecast. The query fixes all three, so these are
robustness comparisons rather than hidden answer paths.

Boundaries: the shared decay is identified by a global minimum on a declared compact
interval, so it is a panel fit rather than a market-implied parameter. The VAR(1)
spectral radius of 0.9848 sits close to the unit circle on 252 observations, so its
stability is a diagnostic rather than an established property, and one next-date
comparison cannot establish forecast skill.

docstring:
Bootstrap a Treasury curve, reprice an auctioned note and hedge key rates.

The selected security is the highest-bid-to-cover original nominal ten-year
note issued in 2025: CUSIP 91282CNC1.  Its issue-date CMT observations are par
yields rather than zero rates.  The case therefore requires a semiannual
par-instrument bootstrap before cash-flow pricing.  Treating the quoted par
yields directly as spot yields is a measured convention error and changes the
note price, duration, convexity, key-rate hedge and next-day result.

The analytical curve is a benchmark construction rather than the unpublished
Treasury production curve.  It linearly interpolates quoted par yields onto a
half-year grid, bootstraps discount factors, and reprices every synthetic par
instrument to numerical zero residual.  The selected note is valued at its
issue date with twenty regular half-year periods and no accrued interest.  Its
auction price was set before settlement, so the model-minus-auction gap is a
descriptive curve/quote reconciliation, not a pricing error.

The final hedge uses synthetic five- and ten-year par securities.  A one-basis-
point bump is applied to one quoted par node at a time, followed by a full
rebootstrap.  Hedge notionals solve the two key-rate equations.  The following
business-day revaluation holds coupons and maturity grids fixed, so it isolates
the observed curve change and is not a realized total return.

Numeric validation uses the shared rounding-boundary tolerance.  Duration and
convexity also admit the pre-registered values obtained from the three otherwise-
correct prices as reported to six decimals; this is a reporting-boundary
equivalence, not an alternative curve convention.  The curve repricing and hedge
residuals are explicit PV invariants.

The `treasury_par_bootstrap_hedge` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to treating
reported par yields as spot rates instead of bootstrapping them, to valuing on the
auction rather than the issue date, and to reporting DV01 as a signed price change
rather than a price loss. The curve method is the one worth naming: skipping the
bootstrap changes every discount factor, so it moves the model price the auction
comparison is built on rather than only the hedge. The query fixes all three, so these
are robustness comparisons rather than hidden answer paths.

docstring:
Rank-one error-correction model for the ten-year yield and speculative positioning.

The ten-year yield, the two-year yield and SOFR move together because they are all
anchored to the same policy path, so a regression in levels between them is
near-spurious while a regression in differences throws the anchor away. An
error-correction model keeps both: a cointegrating relation in levels plus an adjustment
term that pulls the yield back toward it.

Over 261 weekly observations from 2021-01-05 to 2025-12-30 the deepest inversion is
2023-07-03 at -1.08 percentage points, with SOFR at 5.06 percent and leveraged-money net
share at -30.448258 percent of open interest. The fitted cointegrating relation puts a
0.5681 coefficient on the two-year yield and only 0.0202 on SOFR, with an
equilibrium error standard deviation of 0.2069 percentage points. The augmented
Dickey-Fuller coefficient on that error is -0.1103 with a t statistic of -3.1434,
so mean reversion is present but the evidence for it is not overwhelming.

The error-correction equation adjusts at -0.0978 per week, roughly a ten-week
half-life, and explains 62.3818 percent of weekly changes with a maximum normal moment
of 0.0. Out of sample over 105 weeks it beats a random walk, 0.0948 against
0.1118 percentage points of root-mean-square error, an improvement of 0.0170.
That margin is small: the model wins by about fifteen percent of the random walk's error,
which is a real but modest edge, and its own worst week, 2025-04-08 at 0.2609
percentage points, is more than twice its average error. Leveraged-money net share on
that date is -38.307589 percent, a more negative position than at the deepest inversion.

The `treasury_rank1_vecm` pinned-reading comparison records sensitivity to the positioning report
scope, to the training-window end, and to whether the regressors are dated
contemporaneously or lagged. The query fixes all three, so these are robustness
comparisons rather than hidden answer paths.

Boundaries: the cointegrating vector is estimated rather than tested for rank, so a
single relation is imposed by the question and not established by a trace or maximum
eigenvalue statistic. The Dickey-Fuller statistic is reported on a residual from an
estimated relation, which changes its distribution, so it is a diagnostic rather than a
size-correct test. Positioning is a weekly reported aggregate across all leveraged-money
accounts and is not a directional forecast; nothing here identifies causality in either
direction between positioning and yields.

docstring:
What a sector transacted and what its holdings are worth are two different series.

The Financial Accounts publish one instrument as several series that share nine
digits and differ only in a two-letter prefix. Corporate equities on the
nonfinancial corporate balance sheet carry LM for the market-value level, FU for
the quarter's own transactions, FA for those same transactions restated at a
seasonally adjusted annual rate, and FR for the revaluation of what was already
held. The change in the level is the sum of the last two, not any one of them:

    LM(t) - LM(t-1) = FU(t) + FR(t)

It closes on all 41 quarter-over-quarter changes the newest release supports,
with a largest absolute residual of 0.0000 million USD. Only four quarterly
series in that release carry an other-volume-change leg at all, so the two-term
form is the ordinary case rather than a simplification.

The trap is which series answers "how much did the sector transact", and it
fires in the first turn. The pinned answer sums FU to -1,050,755.0000 million
USD. Summing FA instead returns -4,203,020.0000 million, exactly four times as
much, because the annual-rate series scales one quarter of activity to a yearly
pace rather than accumulating four quarters of it. Reading the change in the
level as the transacted amount returns +1,689,557.0000 million and carries the
opposite sign. At four requested decimals the rounding-boundary tolerance is
0.00006 million USD against separations of 3,152,265.0000 and 2,740,312.0000, so
neither wrong figure can enter the accepted band. The wrong path changes the
summed-issuance output in the first turn; the second turn's counts and the third
turn's comparison are computed per quarter from the same legs and are reached
through the identity, which is what exposes the substitution. The fourth turn
names the ratio openly, after the first turn has been scored.

The financial point is that the sector was shrinking its equity while the market
value of that equity grew. Net issuance is negative in 33 of the 41 quarters --
buybacks and cash acquisitions exceeding placements -- and net issuance and the
market-value change carry opposite signs in 21 of them. The revaluation is the
larger term in 37. Anyone reading the balance-sheet line as a measure of what
corporations did would conclude they raised 1.69 trillion USD of equity over the
decade, when they retired 1.05 trillion.

The revaluation leg is not a plug. Expressed against the market value each
quarter opened with, it correlates 0.9936 with the value-weighted market return
compounded over that quarter's trading days, differs from it by a median 0.5186
percentage points and agrees in sign in 39 of 41 quarters. That is the check the
second source exists for; the accounts alone cannot supply it.

Fragility: the largest absolute revaluation, -484,583.0000 million on
2022-06-30, stands only 5.82 percent ahead of the runner-up at -457,935.0000
million on 2020-03-31, so that selection is a two-quarter race rather than a
wide margin. The frozen release fixes it.

Only the newest release is read, and that pin is load bearing rather than
decorative: every earlier release in the extract disagrees with it on between 16
and 32 of this instrument's observations, by as much as 650,435 million USD.
Differencing the same series across releases measures revision, which four cases
in this suite already ask about and which this one deliberately avoids.

Two further conventions are left out of the query because they change nothing.
The level appears in three or four statement tables at once and every copy
carries the same value, so which copy is read cannot move an answer. And no two
quarters share a revaluation magnitude, so the tie rule the query states has
nothing to break here.

Numeric validation uses the shared 0.6 x 10^-N rounding-boundary tolerance for N
requested decimals; counts match exactly and the quarter end is compared as a
string. Summed money figures are stable to 0.0000000000 across sixteen
summation orders.
